items.cleanReaderHtml:
Avi Davidson lost his left hand as a teenager. Since then, he’s cycled through a few prosthetics. But his latest is different—it’s wired up to nerves in the upper part of his forearm and allows him to feel pressure. For the first time in years, he can use his left limb to handle delicate objects like grapes, eggs, and a loved one’s hand.

Davidson, who is taking part in a clinical trial run by the University of Utah, is the ninth person to have this experimental device implanted in his arm. But he’s the first to take it home and use it independently.

The hand is part of the bionic LUKE arm, named after Luke Skywalker of Star Wars, who was fitted with a lifelike prosthetic arm after his own was light-sabered off. The arm was developed in the 2000s, initially trialed in 2014, and approved by the FDA that same year. The trial that Davidson is enrolled in isn’t so focused on the arm itself but on a new way to connect it to a person’s nervous system. The connection allows users to control movements and receive feedback about how much pressure they’re applying.

Researchers hope that Davidson’s experiences will help them answer some long-standing questions about the technology, including how useful it really is in day-to-day life. They want to know when the device is helpful and where it might fail. They also want to learn how it might affect Davidson’s well-being as well as his brain and nervous system.

In 2009, when he was 16, Davidson climbed a telephone pole to get the best shot of a sunset. “I climbed about 35 feet up,” he recalls. But he lost his footing as he tried to descend. He grabbed for a wire, which ended up electrocuting him, before he fell to the ground.

The accident resulted in second- and third-degree burns over 37% of his body, says Davidson, “and I broke my back in approximately 50 separate locations.” He also broke eight ribs, and his spinal cord was severed. He’s pretty sure he broke his left wrist, too. But around 10 days later, his left hand—his dominant hand, and the one he’d grabbed the wire with—had started to develop gangrene. It was amputated.

Davidson was ultimately in a coma for around a month. “Once I woke up, they explained to me: You’re paralyzed, you’re never going to walk again, and also, we took your left hand,” he recalls. “A bit of an inconvenience at 16, to say the least.”

Davidson, now 33 and a trauma therapist, went on to have physical therapy and adjusted to life in his changed body. He’s tried a range of prosthetic hands. The first one, which he received a year and a half after his injury, was a basic hook that allowed him to pick things up. It wasn’t fancy, but it gave him “a psychological feeling of returning to being whole,” he says.

The hands he’s tried since have been more advanced—some have allowed him to control individual fingers with muscle movements, for example. Some have been covered by his medical insurance, which allows for replacements around every five years, he says. Others he’s had to buy himself. He bought his third prosthetic hand, for example, from eBay. “It’s funny to think I bought a secondhand second hand,” he says.

A chance encounter with a scientist at a supermarket introduced Davidson to the research team at the University of Utah, which specialized in researching devices that plug into the body. Since 2013, the team had been running a trial of a system that could connect with the nerves of a residual limb, allowing an amputee to control a bionic one. Davidson turned out to be an ideal candidate, says Jake George, director of the university’s neurorobotics lab.

Davidson, who was keen to take part, first had to undergo what George describes as “pretty extensive” physical and psychological evaluations. Not only did he have to be well enough for surgery, but the team also scanned his brain to make sure that he still had a mental representation of his left hand—suggesting he’d be able to move a bionic one. They also ran tests to check that the nerves in his arm were working.

A therapist evaluated Davidson’s motivations for taking part in the trial. “Our patients aren’t being compensated, they don’t get to keep the device, and they go through two surgeries—the surgery to get it in and the surgery to take it out,” says George. “Avi’s doing this because he wants to help others.”

In late January of this year, Davidson flew from Florida to Utah to undergo his first surgery. It was a fairly complicated procedure involving engineers as well as a full surgical team. “We [researchers] stand in the back of the room and basically answer the question when the surgeon asks, ‘Where do I put the damn thing?’” says George. The surgeon exposed three nerves in Davidson’s arm and implanted an electrode array containing 100 needles in each one.

Nerves are floppy, so pushing electrodes into them doesn’t do much, says George. Instead, the team connected the electrodes to the nerves using what he describes as a “compressed-air gun.” “You shoot the grid of needles into the nerve at a very, very high velocity,” he says.

The team also inserted 24 electrodes into the muscles around the nerves. Wires for each of the nerve arrays and for pairs of muscle electrodes were left protruding from Davidson’s skin. After the surgery, he was offered some time to recover. “By day two, I’m like ‘No, let’s get me on the machines,’” he says.

That next step involved training a computer system to essentially translate the electrical activity in Davidson’s nerves into signals for bionic hand and wrist movements.

To get it up and running, the team had to train the device in two directions. The first involved converting nerve activity into hand, wrist, and finger movements. The researchers did this by listening in on the signals collected from the hundreds of electrical connection points in Davidson’s arm while he thought about various movements. That part was easy, says George: “It takes a matter of about five minutes.”

The second direction—linking the electrodes to sensations felt by the prosthetic—is much more time-consuming. Team members would stimulate each of the electrode connection points in turn, asking Davidson if he felt anything. They’d then turn up the signal at each of those points to see the effect. “It’s like a three-day process,” says George.

Davidson’s wires have since been connected and simplified, says George, who describes the process as “more or less like plugging in an HDMI cord or a USB-C cord.” When he wants to use his prosthetic, Davidson must first put it on, connect it to the wires, and then initiate it using a small computer.

He’s also had to undergo extensive physical therapy to learn how to control the hand. After all, it’s nothing like the prostheses he’s used in the past. “It’s almost like learning a different language with this kind of technology,” says Leanne Seckinger, an occupational therapist at the University of Utah Health System, who works with Davidson.

At first, she and Davidson worked on learning to hold and stabilize objects. They focused on Davidson’s personal goals—he wanted to be able to cook at home, so the pair worked on strategies to hold and manipulate utensils, prepare and chop ingredients, and carry plates and bowls. “He was able to crack an egg,” says Seckinger. “He made an omelet.”

Davidson has been using the hand at home since July 10, and he has noticed improvements. At first it took him a few minutes to write his name; now he can manage it in seconds. “The things I’m able to do with it now are tremendous, comparatively to where I was at initially,” he says.

Today, he says, he wears the hand around six days a week. He changes the batteries once or twice during the day and takes it off overnight. It’s heavy, weighing in at around five pounds, he says.

The hand can be useful, but it has also proved surprising. Sometimes, Davidson feels pain in it. This could be what’s known as “phantom pain”—a symptom experienced by some people who have lost a limb.

Curiously, he also says he experiences wrist strain. Davidson says he’s been getting a stiffness in his prosthetic wrist similar to what he experiences when he’s been typing for a long time with his flesh-and-blood right hand. He’s also realized that he can relieve the tension by pulling the bionic fingers back to stretch out his prosthetic wrist. “It’s weird,” he says.

The phenomenon “makes no sense physiologically,” says Chris Duncan, a rehabilitation doctor and chief medical officer at BIOS, a neurotechnology company that is supporting the trial. Stretching a typical hand pulls on tendons that extend down the forearm. There aren’t any tendons in a bionic arm—Davidson’s “stretches” are just moving actuators, says Duncan. He doesn’t know why it’s helpful but suspects it might have something to do with how the hand is represented in his mind. “What Avi’s experiencing is kind of like uncharted territory, honestly,” he says.

The research team is currently planning a bigger study and hopes to get the two-way sensation device approved by the FDA so that it can be covered by health insurance. “They need to understand that this is a useful new technological paradigm that will bring value to patients,” says Duncan. Team members also hope the technology will allow users to operate other devices, such as remote controls and wheelchairs.

items.cleanReaderHtml:
Alice’s Restaurant. It’s now a Thanksgiving classic, and something of a tradition around here. Recorded in 1967, the 18+ minute counterculture song recounts Arlo Guthrie’s real encounter with the law, starting on Thanksgiving Day 1965. As the long song unfolds, we hear all about how a hippie-bating police officer, by the name of William “Obie” Obanhein, arrested Arlo for littering. (Cultural footnote: Obie previously posed for several Norman Rockwell paintings, including the well-known painting, “The Runaway,” that graced a 1958 cover of The Saturday Evening Post.) In fairly short order, Arlo pleads guilty to a misdemeanor charge, pays a $25 fine, and cleans up the thrash. But the story isn’t over. Not by a long shot.

Later, when Arlo (son of Woody Guthrie) gets called up for the draft, the petty crime ironically becomes a basis for disqualifying him from military service in the Vietnam War. Guthrie recounts this with some bitterness as the song builds into a satirical protest against the war: “I’m sittin’ here on the Group W bench ’cause you want to know if I’m moral enough to join the Army, burn women, kids, houses and villages after bein’ a litterbug.” And then we’re back to the cheery chorus again: “You can get anything you want, at Alice’s Restaurant.”

We have featured Guthrie’s classic during past years. But, for this Thanksgiving, we give you the illustrated version.

items.cleanReaderHtml: No es solo un documental al uso, aunque cuente una historia real y filme a su protagonista. No es únicamente un true crime, pero describe los 34 días previos a la entrada a la cárcel de una criminal. No es un reality show, aunque retrata la vida de una familia en un momento de tensión. No es una película de ficción, pero hay una actriz que puede ser candidata al Oscar a mejor interpretación femenina secundaria. You Can See Everything, que en España llevará el subtítulo de Puedes verlo todo, es todo lo anterior, un poco más y, sobre todo, disfruta del mayor hype —en inglés, expectación o bombo publicitario— de la cinefilia de este fin de año. Y eso que dura casi tres horas, que la protagonista ahora mismo está en prisión cumpliendo una pena de 11 años de cárcel y sus dos directores no dan entrevistas. Después de lograr el mejor estreno para un documental no musical en EE UU, ya ha superado los 105 millones de dólares en taquilla, y eso que costó solo siete hacerla. Ese hype ha llegado a España y, por eso, este jueves el filme se verá en casi un centenar de pantallas un mes antes de su estreno comercial. Y en el horizonte está la gala de los Oscar, la meta de una carrera en la que You Can See Everything entra con la mayor de las ambiciones: la estatuilla a mejor película, algo que nunca ha logrado un documental.

items.cleanReaderHtml:
Here we are, living these lives bright and perishable as a poppy, hard and shimmering as obsidian. We know that they are entirely improbable, that we bless that bright improbability with each flash of gratitude for it all, that if we pay attention closely and generously enough we are always repaid in gladness, that it is the handle of the door to the world. And yet over and over we choose to live in the cage of complaint, too preoccupied with how the will of life betrayed our wishes, the wanting monster always growling in the other corner of the cage.

Imagine parting the bars and stepping out. Imagine waking up with a rush of gladness at everything we were never promised but got anyway — trees and music, clouds and consciousness, the cobalt eye of the scallop, the golden fan of the gingko, the alabaster chandelier of the ghost pipe.

In our age of competitive prostration, this is a headstand hard to hold for long. But it is trainable. It is possible to become strong enough to be tender, it is.

Artist and poet Rachel Hébert offers a bright patch of training ground in The Book of Thanks: A Catalogue of Gratitudes — one of the most miraculous books I have ever encountered, trembling with tenacious tenderness for the bewilderment of being alive.

Radiating from the pages is an invitation, extended in paintings and poems, to open “the sunlit fort of your attention” and let the world rush in, in all its minute and majestic loveliness: stalactites and Spanish moss, spiderwebs and skylights, snow and the call of the snowy owl, the heart’s capacity for “an urgent, flashing, interrupting kind of love.”

What emerges is prayerful (“more cellos, touch, and rain, please”) and singing with praise (“roots gripping, canyon carved, spine woven of baleen a thousand years old”) — a manual for how to live in gratitude (“what is working wants your praise”) and a theological statement (“there is nothing you must do to belong”).

What do we say to longing?

If you have sat in the chill
of early morning bleakness

and watched as the deep blue
sighed and blushed, touched

by the warm curve of dawn
and pinker than pink then

apricot soft and spreading its
glow, you know. You know.

How
— in this dim parade of brutality —
might all be well?

But if we trouble it with light,
train our sights on
the rebellious good,

and work
to make it
truer.

Beneath the face
of the water,
wonder.

In dark woods,
a gate.

In the chapter
called lostness,
a friend.

All the help
we could not
yet see.

It cannot be always comfortable.
So love the thousand knives as they enter
and see your shape still sitting.

See that you too belong to paws
of soft silent hungers, to thirst-tangled
roots, to silver-spun constellations.

Know you’re no sicker than the rest of us.
The big secret is this: No one else can brave you.
Messy, yes. And marvelous.

What is more than we see
in this world we’re pressed into,
its blistered barking noise?

For what we build, speak, and ruin —
our efforts, our angers.

For music.

For wings.

For seventeen years, I have been spending hundreds of hours and thousands of dollars each month composing The Marginalian (which bore the outgrown name Brain Pickings for its first fifteen years). It has remained free and ad-free and alive thanks to patronage from readers. I have no staff, no interns, no assistant — a thoroughly one-woman labor of love that is also my life and my livelihood. If this labor makes your own life more livable in any way, please consider lending a helping hand with a donation. Your support makes all the difference.

items.title: The Paradox of “Finding Yourself”
items.author: Maria Popova
items.summary: "The self is a style of being, continually expanding in a vital process of definition, affirmation, revision, and growth..."

items.cleanReaderHtml:
“The self is a style of being, continually expanding in a vital process of definition, affirmation, revision, and growth…”

“No one can build you the bridge on which you, and only you, must cross the river of life,” thirty-year-old Nietzsche wrote in his treatise on how to find yourself. And yet in the century and a half since, a curious dissonance has begun to reverberate across culture: On the one hand, we have grown increasingly fixated on the self as the focal lens for interpreting the world — a fixation which Ian McEwan so brilliantly satirized and which has precipitated today’s tragic epidemic of militant identity politics; on the other hand, the rise of neuroscience has demonstrated again and again that the self we experience as so overwhelmingly real — the psychophysiological raft of experience through which we float along the river of life — is a sensory-perceptual byproduct of consciousness, completely illusory in its solidity.

Nearly half a century ago, the Pulitzer-winning poet Robert Penn Warren (April 24, 1905–September 15, 1989) cast a cautionary eye to the notion of “finding oneself” in Democracy and Poetry (public library) — his magnificent Jefferson Lecture about power, tenderness, and art’s role in a healthy society.

Decades before Harvard psychologist Daniel Gilbert’s witty and wise observation that “human beings are works in progress that mistakenly think they’re finished,” Warren challenges the cultural trend of young people taking “time off” from school or work in order to “get away from it all” and find themselves. He writes:

In the phrase [“to find myself”] lurks the idea that the self is a pre-existing entity, a self like a Platonic idea existing in a mystic realm beyond time and change. No, rather an object like a nugget of gold in the placer pan, the Easter egg under the bush at an Easter-egg hunt, a four-leaf clover to promise miraculous luck. Here is the essence of passivity, one’s quintessential luck. And the essence of absurdity, too, for the self is never to be found, but must be created, not the happy accident of passivity, but the product of a thousand actions, large and small, conscious or unconscious, performed not “away from it all,” but in the face of “it all,” for better or for worse, in work and leisure rather than in free time.

In consonance with my own deep belief in the ongoingness and fluidity of our becoming, Warren adds:

The self is a style of being, continually expanding in a vital process of definition, affirmation, revision, and growth, a process that is the image, we may say, of the life process of a healthy society itself.

In a sentiment that calls to mind Academy of American Poets executive director Jennifer Benka’s beautiful observation that “poems are physical sites of discovery [and] sense-records of our humanity,” Warren considers the role of poetry as a locus of our evolving being:

How does poetry come into all this? By being an antidote, a sovereign antidote, for passivity. For the basic fact about poetry is that it demands participation, from the secret physical echo in muscle and nerve that identifies us with the medium, to the imaginative enactment that stirs the deepest recesses where life-will and values reside. Beyond that, it nourishes our life-will in the process of testing our values. And this is not to be taken as implying a utilitarian aesthetic. It is, rather, one way of describing our pleasure in poetry as an adventure in the celebration of life.

Complement this particular portion of Warren’s thoroughly transcendent Democracy and Poetry with Walt Whitman on identity and the paradox of the self and philosopher Rebecca Goldstein on what makes you and your childhood self the “same” person despite a lifetime of change, then revisit Elizabeth Alexander on what poetry does for the human spirit.

items.cleanReaderHtml:
A conversation with a Salk Institute plant genomicist, and cranberry fanatic, on his research into improving the fate of the Thanksgiving staple

A Thanksgiving staple faces an uncertain future if the weather disruptions wrought by climate change continue to disrupt the harvest. Cranberries, traditionally prepared as sauces or jellies, play a supporting role to roast turkeys and steaming mashed potatoes on many tables across the United States tomorrow.

But in Wisconsin, the region that leads the nation in producing this native North American fruit, some growers are seeing harvests decline as the state’s cranberry bogs have been hit by heat waves, drought, cold snaps, and hailstorms in the past couple of years. Last month, Sondra Brancel, an appraiser specializing in cranberry marshes, or bogs, and a member of the American Society of Farm Managers and Rural Appraisers, told RFDTV that Wisconsin cranberry growers were expecting reduced yields, as they had last year, attributing the downtick to climatic disruptions.

“For the second year in a row, we’re experiencing a lower harvest,” she said. “Most of that almost always has to do with Mother Nature, of course, like in all aspects of agriculture.”

More recent numbers from the Department of Agriculture indicate that the Wisconsin harvest, which accounts for about 60 percent of the national crop, was somewhat rescued by a late-season harvesting push, with a four percent increase over last year. But the warning signs of a shifting climate worry cranberry farmers and enthusiastic consumers of the fruit alike.

One self-described “cranberry fanatic” is Todd Michael, a plant genomicist at California-based Salk Institute for Biological Studies. Michael and his collaborators published research earlier this year in the journal Plants People Planet that offers a ray of hope to the continued production of cranberries in a changing climate. The scientists experimented with crossing Vaccinium oxycoccos , a wild cranberry relative that grows in northern latitudes, with the cultivated cranberry ( Vaccinium macrocarpon ) that makes its way onto Thanksgiving tables and, more importantly, into leftover turkey sandwiches.

I spoke with Michael about his findings, the wonders of bog-front living, the future of the iconic Thanksgiving fruit, and what about cranberries mesmerizes him.

I’m a cranberry fanatic. We think of cranberries this time of year, because it’s Thanksgiving, and it’s iconic for Thanksgiving because it’s also from the harvest in the fall. I grew up in New Jersey, right on the edge of the bogs, so I’m very familiar with it. I’ve always eaten cranberries. I drink cranberry juice every single day. So it’s just a part of my life.

My first faculty position was at Rutgers University, and as soon as I got there, I reached out to the USDA researchers at the cranberry station wanting to do some of these genomics. Basically, I want to go back to my roots, so to speak.

You say there’s a decrease in cranberry production. Is Vaccinium macrocarpon imperiled in some way? And if so, how is that playing out?

I don’t know if I’d say “imperiled.” Cranberry has been cultivated for 200 years, and there really hasn’t been much breeding done on cranberry. A lot of the varieties that are grown in Massachusetts, which is the second highest producer of cranberries, New Jersey, which is the third, and then Wisconsin, which is the number one producer of cranberries, all have different varieties that are really one step removed from “land races,” or wild selections of cranberry.

There’s a real opportunity to do some breeding in cranberries and for those specific locations. It’s predominantly a bog-grown plant. So both in New Jersey and Massachusetts, it’s like right on the coast in the bog areas.

So imperiled is the wrong word. But as I understand it there are some areas of its traditional range where—I don’t know if endangered is the right word—I think there are places where they’re losing wetland habitat. Is that right?

Oh, yeah. I mean the loss of wetlands is definitely a huge factor in terms of the decrease of the species in general. In Massachusetts, it’s a combination of water and stress from changing climate but also houses—so loss of wetlands or bogs. They do have a pretty aggressive program in Massachusetts at least where they don’t really want bogs to go out of production. So they’re incentivized to either do restoration of bogs or bring them back into a native state instead of building houses.

items.summary: "Gribshunden" was the "floating castle" of King Hans of Denmark and Norway. It exploded and sank in 1495, but the Baltic Sea's low salinity has kept contents remarkably well preserved

items.cleanReaderHtml:
More than five centuries after a royal Danish warship exploded and sank off the coast of Sweden, underwater archaeologists have uncovered finely crafted chain mail armor resting on the Baltic seafloor.

The copper-alloy mail fragments were recovered in October from the wreck of Gribshunden , or Griffin , the 15th-century flagship of King Hans of Denmark and Norway. Researchers discovered the armor alongside a rare munitions chest while surveying the area beneath the vessel’s forecastle, an elevated combat platform at the ship’s bow.

“It was in the process of documenting the chest that I unexpectedly discovered exposed mail-armor fragments in the vicinity of the chest, along other items that could indicate more chests,” Rolf Warming , an archaeologist at Stockholm University who leads the project with Södertörn University’s Johan Rönnby , tells Live Science ’s Kristina Killgrove in an email. “It was only by chance that we came across it, and it shows just how much is still on the wreck site.”

To map the newly explored section of the ship, the researchers paired diver-led excavation with high-resolution 3D photogrammetry and an uncrewed robotic survey boat operating on the surface, according to a statement . Together, the armor, the munitions chest and earlier finds of lead objects possibly linked to ammunition molds could point to a dedicated military storage zone.

“Historical sources indicate that German mercenaries, or Landsknechts , were aboard Griffin when it sank in 1495,” Rodrigo Pacheco-Ruiz , a maritime archaeologist at the University of Southampton and co-investigator on the project, says in the statement. “This part of the ship may therefore have been used to stow equipment associated with these soldiers, including their armor, although we’ve yet to establish a precise function for the space.”

When Gribshunden set sail from Copenhagen in the summer of 1495, it led an 18-ship royal fleet bound for a political summit in Kalmar, Sweden, as Smithsonian magazine’s Jo Marchant reported in 2021. Hans, who ruled Denmark and Norway from 1481 to 1513, hoped to quell Swedish rebels and revive the Kalmar Union , which united the three kingdoms. Acting as both a diplomatic showcase and a “floating castle,” Marchant wrote, the flagship carried Danish noblemen, courtiers, a royal astronomer and roughly 150 German mercenary soldiers.

“It was important to demonstrate military prowess, and the German and Swiss mercenaries were the finest you could get at that time,” Warming tells Live Science .

The voyage ended in catastrophe while the ship lay anchored north of the small island of Stora Ekon, near Ronneby in southern Sweden. Gribshunden erupted in flames and sank rapidly. A 16th-century account of Hans’ life suggests its gunpowder stores accidentally ignited, while other hypotheses point to a possible lightning strike. Many aboard perished in the fire or drowned, though Hans survived because he was ashore at the time.

Rediscovered by local divers in 1971 and formally identified in 2013, the Gribshunden has survived in remarkable condition, thanks to the Baltic Sea’s low salinity, which keeps wood-eating shipworms at bay.

Shipworms—which are actually a type of saltwater clam—have tormented seafarers for centuries. In fact, they may have weakened the hulls of the ships of the Spanish Armada when it failed in attacking England in 1588, leaving the ships vulnerable to cannonballs and storms.

Measuring nearly 100 feet long and resting in about 30 feet of water, the vessel is a rare surviving example of a late-medieval “ caravel ”-style ship, constructed with hull planks laid edge to edge over an internal frame so it could carry heavy cargoes and guns. That design placed Gribshunden in the same technological generation as the vessels sailed by Christopher Columbus and Vasco da Gama . Previous dives also yielded a fearsome carved figurehead depicting a monster swallowing a screaming man.

Despite the exceptional craftsmanship of the newly recovered chain mail, its quality does not automatically tie it to an elite knight or king. “This kind of armor could remain in use for extended periods, often undergoing repairs or being reused, so these fragments may represent older military equipment that was still active,” Warming explains in the statement.

Researchers are now conducting chemical analyses on the armor and on samples taken from the munitions chest to determine the chain mail’s origins and the chest’s contents.

It is actually a really fascinating research question of ours that could illuminate supply chains and the military logistics,” Warming tells Live Science . “Did the mercenary forces bring their own ammunition and tool kit aboard, or was this supplied by the royal fleet?”

items.cleanReaderHtml:
Thanksgiving is upon us, which means it’s time for single people to suffer through awkward questions about why they’re not in a relationship. The good news is that anyone who finds themselves in that uncomfortable position can now refer their nosy relatives to two new studies about singlehood published in this week.

In the first study , sociologists examined what personality traits were linked to being single. They used data from 14 waves of a large-scale longitudinal study in Germany that tracked changes in the big five personality traits and romantic relationship status over time.

Read more: “ When Dating Algorithms Can Watch You Blush ”

They found that personality traits that stayed stable were more likely to predict relationship status than those that shifted over time. Those who scored higher in openness to experience tended to fly solo for longer, an association that was more pronounced in women. People who were more extroverted, conscientious, and agreeable, on the other hand, were more likely to be coupled up. Men who were more extroverted were particularly more likely to have partners. Importantly, the researchers stressed that no one personality type is fated to any romantic relationship status, single or otherwise.

The team also looked at the “Dark Triad” of personality traits: narcissism, psychopathy, and Machiavellianism. People with higher levels of psychopathy and narcissistic admiration (the tendency to self-promote for social status) were less likely to be in a relationship. But those who scored higher for Machiavellianism were more likely to be in a relationship (although there was no data on how happy those relationships were).

“We often assume that single people are all in the same situation, but the reality is much more complex,” Elyakim Kislev of the Hebrew University of Jerusalem, author of both studies, said in a statement. “Personality may help explain why some people are more likely to be single, but it does not tell us whether they are happy. To understand that, we also need to consider how people experience singlehood and the expectations society places on them.”

To do exactly that—that is, to investigate how satisfied singles were with their lives—Kislev turned to survey data from more than 5,000 single adults aged 30 and up from five countries (the United States, United Kingdom, Japan, Mexico, and Spain). Kislev focused on two conflicting aspects of singlehood: the sense of freedom that comes from not being tied down and the social stigma some people feel as a result of being uncoupled.

In all five countries, single people who viewed their lives as more free and independent also reported higher satisfaction with their singlehood. On the other hand, those who said they experienced more pressure to be in a relationship or endured prejudice for not being one were less satisfied with their lives.

Called “singlism” (a term coined in 2005), these perceived negative attitudes toward the uncoupled leave a mark on how they view their lives. Kislev found that people who experienced singlism were less happy to be alone in all five countries, even after taking into account their overall satisfaction levels.

So the next time prying relatives try to meddle in your romantic affairs, just remind them they’re being singlist. It might at least buy you enough time to extricate yourself from the conversation.

Can this “deadly sin” help cultivate a constructive drive to better ourselves?

items.author: David Nield

items.cleanReaderHtml:
Not the most aesthetically pleasing look, but essential for survival

Researchers have discovered a new dwarf sperm whale species, now extinct, that dates back six million years to the Late Miocene period—and there’s something particularly unusual about it.

The species, Scaphokogia huachafo , is described as having a “completely crooked” skull. Both nostrils are shifted way over to the left of the face, while the rest of the skull structure is distinctly asymmetrical as well, with a downward-curving head. It may be the most extreme facial asymmetry seen in any known mammal to date, and it’s recently been recorded in a study published in Communications Biology .

At first, the researchers weighed the possibility that the fossil that was discovered in the arid Pisco Formation of southern Peru had been distorted or flattened somehow. Yet there was no sign of a fracture or deformation—this is actually how the whale looked.

Its unique appearance helped inspire the whale’s scientific name. The term “huachafo” translates as something extravagant, bizarre, tacky, or over-the-top in Peruvian Spanish. “It broke every rule of symmetry and elegance seen in living cetaceans,” study author Aldo Benites-Palomino explained in a statement . “Its anatomy is so extravagant and odd that huachafo seemed the perfect name for it.”

There is a purpose to the severe asymmetry. Having some of its features off to one side would’ve helped the dwarf sperm whale gobble up food from the seabed, in shallow water around coastlines.

While S. huachafo is no longer with us, it would’ve grown to almost 9 feet in length and could bend its head downwards by 55 degrees according to a skull reconstruction carried out by the research team. “The combination of dense bone, the downward-curving snout and the flexible neck articulation allowed the animal to move directly above the seabed and feed close to the sediment,” study author Gabriel Aguirre-Fernández said .

A shift in ocean ecology and aquatic life between the Miocene and Pliocene most likely did S. huachafo in, the researchers suggest, as this way of feeding was no longer viable. But it’s still a reminder of one of the key fundamentals of evolutionary history: Good looks are nowhere near as important as the ability to find good food.

David Nield has written about science and technology for more than 20 years. His work has appeared in a wide range of publications, including Wired, Popular Science, The Guardian , and Gizmodo .

items.title: America's Thanksgiving Parade in Detroit Is Celebrating 100 Years of Elaborate Floats, Papier-Mâché 'Big Heads' and a Distinguished Clown Corps
items.author: Smithsonian Smart News
items.summary: A new exhibition at the Detroit Historical Society looks back at 100 years of the city's Thanksgiving Day parade, which is tied with New York City for the country's second-oldest

images.caption: Imagen principal de Smithsonian Smart News
Imagen en alta resolución de la fuente
Imagen en alta resolución de la fuente
Imagen en alta resolución de la fuente

Distinguished Clown

videos.caption: Enlace audiovisual citado en la nota

items.cleanReaderHtml:
For festive Detroiters, this year’s Thanksgiving Day is cause for a larger celebration than usual. On Thursday morning, the city will host its 100th annual America’s Thanksgiving Parade , marking a major milestone for what is already one of the oldest holiday traditions in the nation.

Founded in 1924, the yearly procession (minus two cancellations due to World War II, in 1943 and 1944) has sent floats, larger-than-life balloons and popular recurring characters down Woodward Avenue in downtown Detroit. This year’s procession will include 33 floats, five giant balloons and seven marching bands, as well as the city’s beloved Big Heads and Distinguished Clown Corps .

Just across town, a second spectacle is also getting in on the fun. Now on display at the Detroit Historical Society , which itself is celebrating its centennial, a new exhibition, “ This is 100: America's Thanksgiving Parade ,” is honoring the cherished parade with a display of historic footage, props and well-known artifacts. Visitors to the installation will have the opportunity to walk through an interactive timeline of the parade’s benchmark moments, try on famous costumes and even sit on the gilded throne of the only person who has featured in the event since the beginning: Santa Claus.

“Santa has been a part of our parade every single year since 1924,” Rebecca Salminen-Witt, the museum’s chief strategy and marketing officer, tells WDIV ’s Jay Scott Smith. “Back in the day, the parade ended right in front of Hudson’s [department store]. Santa would exit his sleigh, he would go upstairs to the 12th floor of Hudson’s and he would open Toy Land for all the children.”

The exhibit features standout pieces from the world’s largest collection of papier-mâché heads, better known as “the Big Heads” in Detroit, which have been worn by performers since the parade’s beginning. Standing between two and four feet tall and weighing between five pounds and 50 pounds, the first masks arrived from the Carnival of Viareggio in Italy and immediately gained notoriety for their eerie look, the Detroit News ’ Francis X. Donnelly reports.

Over the decades, some 300 new masks were made in caricature of celebrities with connections to Detroit, including Aretha Franklin , Bob Seger, Stevie Wonder , Gordie Howe, Barry Sanders and Sparky Anderson. About half of these feature in the parade each year, while the others are kept in a warehouse with other retired parade paraphernalia.

“Members of the Big Head Corps pay $300 apiece and pick out what Big Head costume they want to be,” Tony Michaels, president of the Parade Company , which organizes the event, tells MLive ’s Edward Pevos and Santino Mattioli. “We have a breakfast for them and they march as a team down Woodward Avenue. This year the new Big Head is Jeff Daniels.”

The installation also features several costumes worn by past members of the Distinguished Clown Corps, a group of community and business leaders who march in the parade in clown attire. With each consecutive year they march, members of the Distinguished Clown Corps earn ever-more-detailed colors, patterns and accoutrements.

“The first five years, [the costume] has to be white,” Lena Antoon, a professor at Wayne State University, told CBS Detroit ’s Sandra McNeill in 2023, her eighth year as a distinguished clown. “And then it’s the pattern of your choice.”

The exhibit traces the story of the parade through factoids and trivia from its long history. In 1934, the Detroit Lions played their first annual Thanksgiving Day football game. The parade was televised for the first time in 1947, though it wasn’t until 1966 that the broadcast was in color. Lassie (the TV dog) was the parade’s grand marshal in 1964, and in 1976, the lit candles from a birthday cake float, made to commemorate the parade’s 50th anniversary, set several small fires along the route. In 1985, a Detroit Free Press article reported that “Santa buckled up in his sleigh because of Michigan’s new seat belt law,” per Midbrow ’s Erica Hobbs.

“Both Thanksgiving and football emerged in the 1860s as efforts to reunite a fractured nation in the aftermath of the Civil War,” Smithsonian magazine ’s Gabby Shell writes. “In the nearly two centuries since, the rituals have evolved in tandem, expanding along with the growing nation and adopting its increasingly consumerist character.”

“It really starts out [featuring] like Mother Goose and storybook characters … and then you slowly see pop culture introduced into the parade, where there’s a Donald Duck float or there’s flying saucers and space-inspired things in the 1960s,” Jeremy Dimick, the exhibit’s curator, tells Hobbs for the Detroit News . “It really just becomes a sign of the times into what’s going on in culture; when you look back at it in its totality, it tells the whole history of the city almost through this lens of the parade.”

Detroit’s parade is tied with New York City’s Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade as the second-oldest in the country. Philadelphia’s Thanksgiving parade , which began in 1920, holds the title of the oldest.

“ This is 100: America's Thanksgiving Parade ” is on view at the Detroit Historical Society through January 3, 2027.

items.cleanReaderHtml:
Fall $1,800 Innovate Grants for Art + PhotoFeatured
Innovate Grant awards two $1,800 grants each quarter to one visual artist and one photographer. Nine honorable mentions in each category are also featured on the Innovate Grant platform and join a growing creative community of esteemed artists. Applicants must be 18 years and older, and all media and genres are accepted. All applicants retain the right to the work they submit.
Deadline: 11:59 p.m. PST on December 15, 2026.

Bryson County Retreat Featured
Practicing artists of any background and at any stage of their career are encouraged to apply for a 2027 residency at Bryson County Retreat. Residency periods can be flexible, but month-long stays are suggested. Bryson County is designed to provide ample living and working space and inspirational settings where an artist may work free from the distractions and responsibilities of day-to-day life. The program includes free lodging near tannic dark water lakes, sprawling live oaks, and drooping Spanish moss at the headwaters of the Santa Fe River in north central Florida.
Deadline: Rolling.

Wildlife Photographer of the Year(International)
Alongside its conservation message, this prestigious global competition is hosted by London’s Natural History Museum to champion the work of photographers, whether professional or amateur, young or older, or using top-of-the-range equipment or smartphones. Photographers are eligible for myriad awards, with a Grand Title prize of £15,000. The entry fee is £35 (free for Young WPY contest).
Deadline: 11:30 p.m. GMT on December 3, 2026.

Responsa Foundation Open Call for Textile Art(International)
The Responsa Foundation champions projects that create meaningful social impact and foster public engagement. The organization is seeking textile artists to submit work for This Memory, a group exhibition taking place from September 22 to October 3, 2027, at Burgh House in Hampstead.
Deadline: December 4, 2026.

Open Call for Public Art Proposals in Moab(Utah, National)
Moab Arts is accepting proposals for 2027 public art projects. Proposals are welcome for sculpture, murals, three crosswalks, and sticker designs but may include other ideas for different media or locations around the city. Preference is given to local and regional artists.
Deadline: 11:59 p.m. MST on December 6, 2026.

Material Works Art Award 2026(International)
Material Works supports artists through one-time $2,500 awards in exchange for original pieces added to its growing contemporary art collection. The award recognizes artistic excellence and aims to promote career advancement through increasing visibility and exposure. There is a €40 application fee.
Deadline: December 6, 2026, or when the first 300 artworks submitted, whichever comes first.

Call for Mail Art(International)
Hive Center for the Book Arts in Evanston, Illinois, welcomes mail art for the exhibition love|mark, which runs from January 1 to February 27. All submissions must arrive at at the center by December 15 for inclusion in the show.
Deadline: December 15, 2026.

Sony Future Filmmaker Awards(International)
The Sony Future Filmmaker Awards is a major program providing opportunities for creators and filmmakers. The shortlisted filmmakers are flown to Sony Pictures Studios in Culver City, California, to attend an awards ceremony and an industry immersion program. Categories include fiction, nonfiction, animation, immersive, student, and vertical format.
Deadline: 7 a.m. CST on December 15, 2026.

GLEAM 2027 Request for Proposals(International)
Olbrich Botanical Gardens in Madison, Wisconsin, invites proposals for temporary, large-scale, light-based artwork for GLEAM, a public art exhibition. The show will be open to the public from August 28 to October 23, 2027.
Deadline: 11:59 p.m. CST on January 6, 2027.

Visual Arts Prize IDEA – Vila d’Amer(International)
Apply for this inaugural prize open to artists working in all visual arts media. Two winning artworks, with prizes of €3,500 and €1,500, will become part of the permanent International Visual Arts Collection IDEA – Vila d’Amer.
Deadline: January 10, 2027.

360 CHICAGO: CloudWalk Call for Artists(Chicago)
One artist will be selected for this major installation in the CloudWalk gallery atop 875 N. Michigan Ave. The selected artist receives a $10,000 commission, and the winning installation will go on view starting April 2027.
Deadline: January 18, 2027.

World of WearableArt 2027 Competition(International)
Entries are now open for the 2027 WOW Competition in Wellington, New Zealand. Awards consist of NZ$200,000 in prizes, including the Supreme WOW Award of NZ$30,000.
Deadline: February 11, 2027 (international), March 31, 2027 (New Zealand).

The Filmed in Nevada County Grant(International)
To support filmmakers in the production of work in Nevada County, California, Nevada City Film Festival offers grants between $1,000 and $20,000.
Deadline: December 1, 2026.

Southern Prize and State Fellowships for Visual Arts(U.S. South)
The South Arts Southern Prize and State Fellowships acknowledge the highest quality artistic work being created in the American South. The program is open to individual artists living in Alabama, Florida, Georgia, Kentucky, Louisiana, Mississippi, North Carolina, South Carolina, and Tennessee. State Fellowships are $5,000, with one awarded per state. These then compete for two Southern Prize tiers of $25,000 and $10,000.
Deadline: January 15, 2027 (fee waiver request by December 18, 2026).

The Virigina A. Groot Foundation Grants(International)
Each year, the Virginia A. Groot Foundation offers three grants to artists who have exceptional talent and a demonstrated ability in ceramic sculpture or sculpture of diverse mediums. The grants are organized into tiers, with the top award providing $60,000, the second award offering $30,000, and the third awarding $20,000.
Deadline: January 9, 2027.

Foundation for Contemporary Arts Emergency Grants(U.S.)
Emergency Grants provide urgent funding for visual and performing artists and poets who have sudden, unanticipated opportunities to present their work to the public, but there is insufficient time to seek other sources of funding or unexpected expenses are incurred for projects close to completion. Each month, the organization makes approximately 15 to 20 grants in the range of $500 to $3,000 each.
Deadline: Rolling.

National Lottery Project Grants(U.K.)
Both individuals and organizations can apply to Arts Council National Lottery Project Grants. These awards are designed to focus on specific projects with starting and ending dates including festivals and carnivals, dance, libraries, literature, museums, music, theater, or visual arts programs. There is no maximum threshold for the fund.
Deadline: Rolling.

Black Artists Grant(U.K.)
The Black Artists Grant offered by Creative Debuts is no-strings-attached financial support to help Black artists. Selected applicants receive £500, and applications are reviewed monthly.
Deadline: Rolling.

The Adolf and Esther Gottlieb Emergency Grant (International)
This program provides one-time financial assistance to qualified painters, printmakers, and sculptors whose needs resulted from an unforeseen catastrophic incident and who lack the resources to meet that situation. Awardees typically receive $5,000 and up to $15,000.
Deadline: Rolling.

Pollock-Krasner Foundation Grant (International)
The foundation welcomes applications from painters, sculptors, and artists working on paper, including printmakers. Grants are intended for one year and range up to $50,000. The artist’s circumstances determine the size of the grant, and professional exhibition history will be considered.
Deadline: Rolling.

Residencies, Fellowships, & More

Kent Cultural Alliance Spring 2027 SERVICE Residency(U.S.)
Artists are invited to apply for a six-week residency session in Chestertown, Maryland, devoted to the theme of service. Each selected artist will receive a $7,500 stipend for the six-week session, a travel reimbursement up to $1,000, and studio and gallery expense reimbursement up to $1,500.
Deadline: 5 p.m. EST on December 1, 2026.

Charles Allis Art Museum Artist in Residence(International)
Located in Milwaukee’s Lower East Side neighborhood, the Charles Allis Art Museum residency program gives one artist the opportunity to engage with the Allis’ collection of more than 800 historic pieces from the early 20th century. The participant receives an $1,800 honorarium and up to a $400 travel stipend.
Deadline: December 4, 2026.

2026 McKnight Fellowships for Fiber Artists(Minnesota)
Each year, the Textile Center awards two unrestricted $25,000 fellowships to post-emerging Minnesota fiber artists who demonstrate exceptional proficiency, sustained practice, and commitment to the field. Fellowship dates are March 1, 2027, to February 28, 2028.
Deadline: December 7, 2026.

Open AIR Residencies(International)
Open AIR is a Missoula-based nonprofit that brings artists and communities together through place-based residencies and public arts programs across Montana. Sessions currently accepting applications include summer 2027, fall 2027, and spring 2028.
Deadline: December 7, 2026.

Cove Park Awarded Residencies for 2027-28(International)
Located in beautiful Argyll & Bute, Scotland, Cove Park awards funded residencies, in addition to travel, visa, materials, and access allowances when required. (Self-funded Open Residencies and subsidized winter residencies are open on a rolling basis.)
Deadline: December 11, 2026.

An Talla Solais Càirdeas/The Kinship Residency(International)
BIPOC artists working in any medium are invited to apply to this fully funded residency in Ullapool in the Scottish Highlands. The program runs throughout January, February, and March 2027. The residency covers all work space, housing, mentoring, and exhibition costs in addition to a £750 weekly stipend.
Deadline: December 14, 2026.

Joshua Tree Highlands Artist Residency 2027-28(International)
Joshua Tree Highlands Artist Residency offers time and space amidst the natural beauty of Joshua Tree National Park. Seven-week residencies include scholarship funds, housing, and studio space designed to accommodate a broad range of artistic activity and open studio events. There is a $45 application fee.
Deadline: December 15, 2026.

items.title: How data centers are driving a US natural-gas boom
items.author: Casey Crownhart
items.summary: In May 2025, my colleague David Rotman wrote a feature story describing how AI could keep us dependent on natural gas. Just 18 months later, I’ve lost count of how many times he’s already been proved right. Sure, it’s technically possible to meet the world’s rising electricity demand with other power sources, including

images.caption: Imagen en alta resolución de la fuente
An aerial view of the Richland Parish Data Center.

items.cleanReaderHtml:
In May 2025, my colleague David Rotman wrote a feature story describing how AI could keep us dependent on natural gas. Just 18 months later, I’ve lost count of how many times he’s already been proved right.

Sure, it’s technically possible to meet the world’s rising electricity demand with other power sources, including renewables like wind and solar supported by batteries. But the reality in the US so far is that the data center boom is helping to fuel a massive natural-gas resurgence.

Just one example: Plans for the Meta data center in Louisiana that David focused on in his story have expanded, and its power needs have too. The local utility went from three planned natural-gas plants to 10. And as I wrote in a new story this week, data center developers are now looking beyond the grid and planning to build their own off-grid gas power plants. How did we get here? 

If you want to understand the future of the grid, one way to do it is by looking at interconnection queues—lists of power plants that have requested a connection to the system. In recent years these queues have been dominated by renewables like wind and solar power, which are generally the cheapest way to build new energy capacity today.

But there’s been a shift in some places, particularly for PJM, the country’s largest power grid operator, which covers parts of 13 states in an area stretching from Illinois to Washington, DC. PJM has seen a major uptick in natural-gas proposals. In August, the operator announced that it had accepted proposals for 715 total projects with a capacity of over 200 gigawatts to join its queue. Nearly half that total capacity represented natural-gas plants.

If all the projects in the queue were built, it would increase the fossil-fuel share on PJM’s grid from 61% to 67%, according to an analysis by Kevin Kircher, an energy modeler and assistant professor of mechanical engineering at Purdue.

PJM’s queue is reflective of a bigger trend across the US. Natural gas is already the single biggest source of electricity in the country, and it has basically become the default to meet exploding power demand.

This AI-driven rush is already affecting greenhouse-gas emissions for tech companies. Meta’s emissions are up 45% over last year’s, according to the company’s recently released 2026 Sustainability Report. That’s even higher than the jumps from fellow hyperscalers Google (18%), Amazon (16%), and Microsoft (25%). The company is also “reevaluating” its 2030 goal to reach net-zero emissions, according to the report, though there aren’t details about how or when it might reach a decision there.

And there’s another tidbit in that Meta report worth noting: The company said that when the grid can’t deliver power “on the necessary timeline,” it will look to other methods, including building its own on-site power generation.

This fits into a related and growing trend that I’ve been tracking recently: Data center developers are looking to bypass long wait times to hook up to the grid by building their own power plants instead.

It’s not new for large industrial facilities to supply their own power. Chemical plants often have natural-gas infrastructure on-site to generate electricity and heat, for example (though they’re generally connected to the grid as well). Mining operations are often remote, requiring an off-grid power source.

But the desire to come online quickly means there could be a massive boom in off-grid power plants for data centers. Over 100 such facilities have been proposed in the US, with a total capacity of 115 gigawatts (that’s more than double the entire peak power demand of California). The vast majority of these sites have been proposed since the beginning of 2025.

There are alternative ways to help meet growing electricity demand: Wind and solar are inexpensive options, and pairing them with batteries could improve their reliability, for example. I’ve also written before about demand flexibility—efforts to limit power drawn from the grid when demand is high. 

Right now, though, the evidence continues to stack up that the AI boom in the US is basically synonymous with a natural-gas boom.

items.title: Astronomers Accidentally Find a Rare Triple-Star System That They Say Shouldn't Exist. It's Located Just 28 Light-Years From Earth
items.author: Smithsonian Smart News
items.summary: The system, called Welopō'ai, includes a red dwarf and two white dwarfs. One of the white dwarfs—a dense stellar leftover—is extremely close to the reddish-orange star, and scientists say the progenitor star that died should have engulfed the red dwarf

images.caption: Imagen principal de Smithsonian Smart News
Imagen en alta resolución de la fuente
Imagen en alta resolución de la fuente
Imagen en alta resolución de la fuente
Margherita Bassi
diagram of the system with zoomed-in part

videos.caption: Enlace audiovisual citado en la nota

items.cleanReaderHtml:
Astronomers searching for exoplanets—worlds beyond our solar system—accidentally uncovered something much stranger. The team stumbled upon an odd triple-star system located merely 28 light-years from Earth. The findings, described November 19 in the journal Astronomy & Astrophysics , challenge scientists’ understanding of how stellar systems work, since this weird one shouldn’t be possible based on our current knowledge.

“It’s a freak thing. It was an annoying object,” lead author Étienne Artigau , an astrophysicist at the University of Montreal in Canada, tells CBC News ’ Nicole Mortillaro. “It’s not what we were looking for.”

Artigau and colleagues had been hunting for faraway planets with a special instrument on the Canada-France-Hawaii Telescope on Mauna Kea, a volcano on Hawaii’s Big Island. It helps researchers identify distant worlds by measuring minuscule changes in a star’s velocity, which can be caused by orbiting planets. But when the instrument turned toward a neighboring red dwarf, a small, cool, orange-ish type of star , the scientists found that its velocity variations were much greater than expected—more than 1,000-fold.

“Typically, we measure fluctuations in a star’s velocity of just a few meters per second. In this case, however, we detected a shift of nearly 16 kilometers per second,” study co-author Atanas Stefanov , an astrophysicist at the University of Geneva in Switzerland, says in a statement . “That was when we realized that what we had encountered was not an ordinary planet, but a much more massive companion.”

Analyses suggested the mysterious satellite must contain more than half the mass of our sun. This high mass and low brightness pointed toward a dead star. So, the researchers conducted follow-up observations in 2023 and 2024 using an instrument on the Gemini North telescope on Mauna Kea. That allowed them to directly detect the culprit behind the dramatic velocity variations: a white dwarf. It’s a dense stellar core left behind by a deceased low- to medium-mass star, like the sun.

This newly discovered white dwarf is quite close to the red dwarf, orbiting at a maximum distance of about 4.6 times the space between the sun and Earth. However, researchers already knew the central star hosted a much more distant white dwarf, and the team estimates it circles the inner pair at about 124 times the distance between our star and our planet. The previously known white dwarf appears to loop around the star duo, while the newly discovered one and the red dwarf orbit close to each other in a binary system.

While astronomers have spotted white dwarf pairs before, Keith Cooper reports for Space.com , a triple system with two white dwarfs and a regular star is exceptionally rare. In fact, this system, dubbed Welopōʻai, is the only one of its kind known in the sun’s neighborhood, according to a separate statement . Astronomers haven’t discovered anything similar within 100 light-years of our planet.

Welopōʻai combines the Hawaiian words welo , meaning an inherited or family trait, and pō‘ai , an orbit or circular path. Together, the name translates to a “path of family traits.”

Welopōʻai is even more mysterious because, according to astrophysicists’ current understanding, it is an impossible stellar system. The star that became the newly discovered white dwarf was originally about 1.4 times as massive as our sun. As it neared the end of its life, it should have ballooned to several hundred times its initial size. Researchers would have expected the enlarging star to engulf the nearby red dwarf and possibly even merge with it .

But surprisingly, that didn’t happen in Welopōʻai. The red dwarf seems to be alive and well, following a wide, stable orbit.

“This system should not exist,” study co-author Patrick Dufour , an astrophysicist at the University of Montreal, says in the second statement. “We have no clean explanation for how it got here. That is the question driving our next observations.”

Even the faraway white dwarf may have once been less of a third wheel, Paul Delaney , an astrophysicist who retired from York University in Canada and wasn’t involved in the study, tells CBC News.

“I would bet that they were relatively proximate to each other and then they did engage in a bit of gravitational embracing, and the farther white dwarf today was much, much closer in its heyday.”

Margherita Bassi is a freelance journalist and trilingual storyteller. Her work has appeared in publications including BBC Travel, Discover magazine, Live Science , Atlas Obscura and Hidden Compass .

items.title: Scientists Discover Signs of Explosive Volcanic Eruptions 20,000 Feet Underwater—the Deepest Ever Found—in the Mariana Trench
items.author: Smithsonian Smart News
items.summary: The discovery puzzles researchers because volcanic activity at that depth should produce a goopy, seeping flow due to the immense pressure. Nevertheless, they say they've found evidence of explosive volcanism, thanks to a remotely operated submersible

images.caption: Imagen principal de Smithsonian Smart News
Imagen en alta resolución de la fuente
Imagen en alta resolución de la fuente
Imagen en alta resolución de la fuente
Sarah Kuta
Sarah Kuta

items.cleanReaderHtml:
Challenger Deep, located in the Mariana Trench in the western Pacific Ocean, is the deepest known point on Earth, plunging 35,876 feet—or nearly seven miles—below the water’s surface.

Now, Challenger Deep can add another distinction to its list: the site of the deepest known explosive volcanic eruptions on Earth. Using a remotely operated underwater vehicle, scientists recovered pyroclastic rocks and “abundant” evidence of ultradeep explosive volcanism from the site. They described their findings in a study published November 22 in the journal Frontiers in Earth Science .

The discovery is “surprising and unprecedented,” William Chadwick , a geologist at Oregon State University who was not involved with the work, tells Science News ’ Carolyn Gramling. “Imagining this happening is … pretty mind-boggling.”

Challenger Deep is a dangerous place for humans to visit, with roughly 1,000 times the pressure we experience at sea level. So, scientists often turn to robots to explore this mysterious submarine depression. In 2024, researchers deployed a Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution submersible called Jason/Medea to explore part of the Mariana Trench.

Some people have made the daring journey to Challenger Deep. The first were U.S. Navy officer Don Walsh and Swiss oceanographer Jacques Piccard , who ventured there in a submarine in January 1960 .

The underwater device couldn’t reach the very bottom of Challenger Deep without risking implosion, but it did descend to a maximum depth of about 21,300 feet. On three dives, the submersible’s camera spotted flat, lobe-shaped rocks at different spots, some located more than about 19,685 feet below the surface, along a 60-mile stretch. Scientists say this material, some of which was brought back to the surface, represents the remnants of a pyroclastic flow, a fast-moving mixture of hot gas, ash and volcanic rock produced by explosive eruptions.

The team couldn’t find the exact location of the eruption, but they suspect it occurred somewhere nearby, along the trench wall. They also don’t know exactly when the eruption occurred, but they think it happened somewhat recently in geologic terms.

“They’re not yesterday, but I don’t think they’re a million years old,” lead author Robert Stern , a geoscientist who retired from the University of Texas at Dallas, tells Live Science ’s Stephanie Pappas.

Most of Earth’s volcanic activity occurs underwater , forming island chains and extensive networks of hydrothermal vents along mid-ocean ridges. But scientists never expected to find explosive eruptions at such extreme depths, thinking they were only possible in shallower waters.

“It’s not something that, as a geoscientist, I would have said would be predicted,” Sune Nielsen , a geochemist at the University of Lorraine in France who was not involved in the study, tells Live Science . “Very far from it.”

In Challenger Deep, explosive eruptions were thought to be impossible, since the immense water pressure should prevent volcanic gases from expanding and triggering an explosion. Yet the evidence suggests some kind of volcanic explosion did occur there, raising new questions about what’s possible.

“Submarine volcanism is something we’ve got quite big knowledge gaps in,” Peter Rowley , a volcanologist at the University of Bristol in England who was not involved with the study, tells New Scientist ’s Matthew Sparkes. “It’s that famous thing that we know less about the seafloor than we do about the moon.”

Scientists still don’t fully understand how explosive volcanism works at such extreme depths. They suspect, however, that these eruptions function very differently than those that occur on land. As Robin George Andrews writes for National Geographic , perhaps an underwater eruption at this depth would look like “a convulsing, crumbling, splintering stream of toothpaste angrily escaping out of the seafloor.”

Another puzzle is the location of the volcanic deposits. Scientists say they sit unusually close to the trench, a subduction zone that began to form about 52 million years ago when the older, denser Pacific tectonic plate started sliding beneath the smaller Mariana microplate.

items.cleanReaderHtml:
Around the dusty plains and otherworldly volcanic rock formations of the historical region of Cappadocia, a millennia-old tradition continues. Here in Central Anatolia, Turkey, horses have been a part of daily life, civic programs, and military campaigns since prehistory. In The Untold Story of the Yilki Horse, photographer Nur Tucker captures a portrait of the region’s living heritage.

Published by Hemeria, the title delves into the beauty and tenacity of the semi-wild horses while also highlighting the lifestyles of those who herd them through rugged landscapes. Tucker, who is a British-Turkish photographer based in the U.K., has long been drawn to the vigor and elegance of horses, and the yilki breed that populates Anatolia have a particularly resonant history.

“Yilki” comes from the Turkish verb yılmak, which means “to flee” or “to be set loose.” The name “has come to describe the condition of these herds that live between liberation and loss, between domestic heritage and wild abandon,” says a statement.

In a place where horses have been bred for agriculture, transportation, battle, and more for thousands of years, their role forever changed within just the past century due to mechanization and industrialization. With motorized tractors, trucks, and cars to work the fields and provide transportation, horses essentially became redundant. Released to fend for themselves, they survived harsh winters, bred on their own, and grew into sizable herds. In The Untold Story of the Yilki Horse, Tucker composes a love letter to these striking animals, celebrating their resilience through more than 100 images.

The book is available for purchase directly from Hemeria, and it’s slated for worldwide release next October. See more on Tucker’s Instagram.

items.cleanReaderHtml:
In Shanghai’s Jing’an Sculpture Park, a monumental new installation by Brooklyn’s Wade and Leta has a clear goal: to get people up and moving in the same space. Titled “Catching Feelings,” the interactive artwork doubles as an all-ages playground with the artists’ signature sculptures and geometric forms. A central tower holds a quartet of slides, while other spinning and writhing elements are designed for more unstructured interaction.

“Catching Feelings” is one of 36 projects in the ninth edition of the Jing’an International Sculpture Project, an annual project helmed by the UCCA Center for Contemporary Art. In comparison to the artists’ earlier works, the bold, kinetic playground is decidedly analog, with any movement powered by the people interacting with its components rather than embedded motors or motion generated by the wind.

“We’re interested in the life and activity around our work—the behaviors it causes, the elations it brings,” the artists say in a statement. “We watched the same grandfather return with his granddaughter to play hide and seek; an 84-year-old and his partner used the space as the backdrop for their video recordings; new friends were made on our ground spinners; we even glimpsed a man in a business suit having a go on the slide.”

“Catching Feelings” is presented alongside monumental works by Olafur Eliasson, Marshmallow Laser Feast, and many others on view through December 31. Find more from Wade and Leta on their Instagram.

items.title: Novel Experiments Expand the Hunt for ‘Ultralight’ Dark Matter
items.author: Jay Bennett
items.summary: Scientists are inventing new ways to search for the missing mass of the universe. The post Novel Experiments Expand the Hunt for ‘Ultralight’ Dark Matter first appeared on Quanta Magazine

images.caption: Lámina de Quanta Magazine

items.cleanReaderHtml:
Click to tell Google to prioritize Quanta and see more of the best coverage of science and math in your search and AI results.

Almost a century ago — in 1933, to be exact — Fritz Zwicky’s studies of distant galaxies led him to suggest that “dark matter is present in very much greater density than luminous matter.” Observations by the astronomer Vera Rubin would later substantiate the case for the intangible, leading her to write in 1980 that “the conclusion is inescapable that non-luminous matter exists.” The elusive stuff appears to react with ordinary matter only through gravity, allowing scientists to estimate how much of it there is. Beyond that, we know very little.

That’s not for lack of trying. Elaborate detectors across the globe have failed to catch any glimpse of dark matter. If you also consider dark energy , which accelerates the expansion of the cosmos, “more than 90% of the matter-energy contents of the universe are unknown,” said Atsushi Taruya , an astrophysicist at Kyoto University in Japan. “That’s a bit embarrassing.”

As null results pile up, scientists are expanding the search, particularly for the tiniest candidates, called ultralight dark matter. Some of the more inventive experiments involve clouds of atoms in quantum superpositions, minuscule levitating magnets, nuclear atomic clocks, and Earth’s geomagnetic field itself. One of these approaches may yield a clue to a whole new realm of physics.

Ultralight dark matter wasn’t always a popular target. For decades, the leading candidate was a “weakly interacting massive particle,” or WIMP, but tests have steadily ruled out WIMPs with different characteristics. In September 2026, researchers working on an experiment called Lux-Zeplin said they had detected a mysterious particle collision in an underground vat of liquid xenon. The cause could have been a WIMP, but many scientists remain skeptical because the collision was so energetic — if WIMPs can have that much energy, several lower-energy collisions should have been detected already. As with other compelling apparent WIMP detections, the peculiar signal may have been a false alarm caused by rare interactions with background particles or a flaw in the data analysis.

A tiny magnet, less than a millimeter wide, levitates in a vacuum. A bump from ultralight dark matter would amplify the natural swaying of the magnet.

Dennis Uitenbroek and Tjerk Oosterkamp, Leiden Institute of Physics

The September blip could end up marking one of the last gasps of the WIMP era. For years now, WIMP searches have been giving way to the hunt for lighter particles — particles so wispy that they would behave more like immense waves flowing through space.

For many scientists, the most appealing ultralight dark matter candidate is the axion. Named in the 1970s for a laundry detergent, this hypothetical particle would clean up a major problem in physics.

The problem concerns the neutron, which is made up of fundamental particles called quarks with opposing electrical charges. According to theories governing the strong nuclear force — the force that holds together atomic nuclei — these charges should be slightly offset. But precision measurements find them almost perfectly aligned, a mystery known as the strong CP problem. A hypothetical field of axions would pull the neutron’s internal charges into the observed alignment.

But searching for axions is a painstaking process. If they account for all or most dark matter, theories suggest that a single axion should be about a trillionth to a billionth of the mass of an electron. So far, physicists have explored only a tiny fraction of these possibilities.

It’s possible that … there’s a whole other world out there that is not, at the moment, visible to us.

One axion-hunting tool is a haloscope, a hollow device with conductive metal walls placed inside a strong magnetic field. If axions from space fly through the magnetic field inside this cavity, they should convert to photons, producing an electromagnetic signal that the experiment would amplify.

The challenge is that, for every possible axion mass, you need a different size detector. For the lighter axions, the cavity needs to have a diameter about that of a beer keg. For heavier axions, you need a smaller cavity. Haloscopes such as the Axion Dark Matter Experiment at the University of Washington have thoroughly searched much of the lighter range without finding anything.

items.title: Meet Earth's New 'Mini-Moon' 2026 QQ8, a Six-Foot-Wide Asteroid That's Temporarily Circling Our Planet
items.author: Smithsonian Smart News
items.summary: An astronomer first spotted the object in August, but scientists needed several weeks to determine whether it was natural or human-made. Earth's gravity captured 2026 QQ8 in April, and the space rock will leave us in December or January

images.caption: Imagen principal de Smithsonian Smart News
Imagen en alta resolución de la fuente
Imagen en alta resolución de la fuente
Imagen en alta resolución de la fuente
Sara Hashemi
Sara Hashemi

items.cleanReaderHtml:
Earth has a new “mini-moon”—at least for another few weeks.

The temporary companion, dubbed 2026 QQ8, entered orbit around our planet in April. Though it was first observed back in August by Hungarian astronomer Krisztián Sárneczky , scientists needed time to confirm whether the object was human-made or celestial. People previously mistook the European Space Agency’s Gaia observatory for a mini-moon, after all, according to Asa Stahl at the Planetary Society .

Finally, on October 29, the International Astronomical Union’s Minor Planet Center announced that the object is, indeed, a space rock. It’ll keep circling Earth until sometime in December or January, after which it will continue its regular orbit around the sun.

According to the Minor Planet Center, the object is only about six feet in diameter. Astronomers doubt it poses any danger to Earth, but even if it did get too close, it’s so small that it would probably burn up in our planet’s atmosphere. It’s also orbiting us from fairly far away—roughly 1.5 times the average distance of the moon, Joanna Thompson reports for Live Science .

This tiny traveler isn’t our first mini-moon, which is an informal term. When little objects pass by Earth, they occasionally get captured by our planet’s gravity. They spend less than a year, on average, orbiting us before being flung back into space. Many scientists speculate that we always have at least one mini-moon. A study published last year even suggests Earth hosts at least six of them at any given time. Despite those postulations, only four other mini-moons have previously been observed, since they’re so small and hard to detect, per the Planetary Society.

Sárneczky, a research coordinator at the Konkoly Observatory in Hungary, says he spotted 2026 QQ8 while “searching for near-Earth asteroids, as I have done on every clear night since 2020.”

“At the time of its discovery, it appeared just like the nearly 400 other near-Earth asteroids I had found,” he tells Jacopo Prisco at CNN . “Its unique nature only became apparent later, following the precise orbital calculations.”

That triggered a weeks-long study by astronomers trying to determine the object’s nature, per the outlet. With the help of the Lowell Discovery Telescope in Arizona and the University of Hawaii’s telescope on Mauna Kea, they confirmed it was born in space.

These objects are asteroids that, from a certain point of view, appear to behave like a moon of Earth, according to the Planetary Society. However, they’re actually orbiting the sun—their orbital paths are just very similar to our planet’s.

According to Live Science , the current mini-moon is classified as an Aten asteroid, a type of space rock whose orbit around the sun occasionally brings it close to Earth. 2026 QQ8 cozies up with our planet around once every ten years. Although this object’s exact origins are unclear, scientists believe most near-Earth asteroids originate in the main asteroid belt , between Mars and Jupiter.

With new telescopes scanning the heavens, scientists expect many more mini-moons to be discovered. For instance, the Vera C. Rubin Observatory in Chile started its decade-long Legacy Survey of Space and Time (LSST) over the summer, and the telescope has already detected thousands of new asteroids as it watches the Southern Hemisphere sky.

“When the LSST survey starts operating fully, it’s expected to discover lots and lots of things,” says Matthew Payne , director of the Minor Planet Center and an astrophysicist at the Center for Astrophysics, Harvard & Smithsonian, to CNN. “The expectation is that we’ll go from knowing 1.5 million objects to knowing 5 million.”

Sara Hashemi is a science writer and fact-checker currently based in New York City. Her work has appeared in Sierra , The Body , Maisonneuve magazine and more.

items.title: The Ten Best Books About Food of 2026
items.author: Smithsonian Arts & Culture
items.summary: Food can provide comfort, and so can cookbooks and food-related memoirs—especially this batch, many of which explore how food can be a salve for mental health

images.caption: Imagen principal de Smithsonian Arts & Culture
