Preview thumbnail for
Preview thumbnail for

items.cleanReaderHtml:
The best part about most cookbooks isn’t necessarily the recipes, but the stories that explain the origin of the recipes. This year’s list of our favorite food books leans into that, featuring ten books that focus on extended narratives on a variety of topics, often on the interconnection of food, lifestyle and mental health. Most of these aren’t the typical cookbooks that take you to a far-off land or into the kitchen of an elite chef, but meditations on why we eat what we do and how it can make us feel. Others expound on surprising topics, like science, immigration, poetry, true crime and … defunct Disney restaurants?

In this book, cookbook author and YouTube personality Carla Lalli leans more on the stories surrounding the end of her quarter-century marriage than neat, tidy recipes. It’s a memoir with recipes; the essays are about coping and grieving and recovering, and each essay is followed by recipes that match the mood, from Heart-Shaped Chicken Cutlets to Separation Pork Chops and a Personal Pot of Beans and Greens. The collection features about 60 recipes—some are more of a vibe than a dish, to be honest, but that’s part of the theme. And if you decide to make one of the recipes in the book, Lalli invites you to make it your own, the best you can under the circumstances you find yourself in. She extends the grace she gave herself during those hard times: “With confidence and freedom, I bequeath you the longest rein.”

One thing to make: Just Like an Olive Oil Cake, but With Sesame Instead

Lydia Pang, a creative director and author who worked with major brands before establishing her own agency , named her memoir after a Chinese idiom that suggests the good things in life are a reward for enduring harder times. Using her own life as a reference point, she contemplates the role food plays in “reflection and realignment,” with each of the eight chapters titled after a dish that she turns into a metaphor for an aspect of her journey—Hot Mess Wontons become a meditation on surrender; Wishbone Tuna on caring. The introduction feels a bit like Crying in H Mart , Michelle Zauner’s acclaimed 2021 memoir, and even includes a reference to Pang breaking down in tears in a Walmart parking lot. (It’s no coincidence: Zauner gets namechecked in chapter 2.) You’ve probably never read a book that used the words “guts” and “sinew” so often, or in as varied contexts; sometimes figurative, sometimes literal.

That a memoir about finding your way as an activist food writer appealed to me is no surprise, but I will admit that I was hesitant to suggest such a specific genre to a wider audience. But here we are, because Alicia Kennedy ’s path was anything but straight, with vignettes of personal growth and loss, as well as professional opportunity and challenges. Her choice to frame each chapter through the lens of a specific food or drink reads as completely natural. A chapter called “On Chocolate,” for instance, is an umbrella to discuss fair-trade initiatives, comforting treats from a grandparent, the dissolution of a relationship and the start of a baking side hustle. With intermingled threads about her dietary choices, her family, her belief system and her career, the book is imbued with humanity and discernment. And her story is so compellingly told that, taken as a whole, it’s easy to find relatable.

There may be no more congenial culinary ambassador than Pati Jinich, who has hosted “Pati’s Mexican Table” on PBS for 15 seasons. This, her fourth cookbook, is a companion to her new series, “ La Frontera ,” documenting life along the U.S.-Mexico border. Of the books on this list, this is the closest to a traditional cookbook, with more than 100 recipes that tell the story of the culture that exists along what she essentially argues is an imaginary line running from the Pacific Ocean to the southern tip of Texas. The book and the series are the culmination of ten years of visiting spots along the nearly 2,000-mile border, with recipes to document the stops along the way.

One thing to make: Any (or all) of the varieties of fish and shrimp tacos she includes

Maybe you’re a good cook and know that you like to grill your steak over high heat and avoid moving it too much so that it develops beautiful grill marks. But do you know why that works better than, say, cooking it over indirect heat? Nik Sharma was a molecular biologist before he became a food writer and photographer, and he can answer that with scientific precision. He takes an elemental approach in this book, organizing chapters based on fire, water, air and earth. It’s also the first cookbook I’ve ever read that genuinely contemplated what cooking in space might look like, building it matter-of-factly into the text, as if that’s something everyone thinks about. The depth and detail he offers in comparing how different scientific principles affect food in different ways—and which you should employ in various scenarios—are staggering. On point, the recipes are tagged to indicate which fundamentals apply to them. Want to make his Crispy Zucchini + Preserved Lemon with Cacio e Pepe? That’s tagged as employing osmosis, boiling and emulsification, all of which Sharma explains.

The social media star ( @blackforager ) commits her enormous personality to the page, offering instruction on eating off the land. Alexis Nikole Nelson has a singular voice and attitude, making her love of foraging infectious. She arranges her advice and instruction by season and by ingredient, and she acknowledges that availability will vary depending on where you’re foraging. The mortal warning of the title is appropriate, but her strategy is to target things that aren’t likely to be confused for anything dangerous. The vegan recipes range from intensely simple (teas and garnishes) to fascinating (a crab cake analogue made with chicken of the wood mushrooms).

In 2020, I predicted that sometime around 2030, we would be hit with a slew of books about how people translated their pandemic-era boredom into successful careers in food and writing. Tanya Bush is a little ahead of that curve. Her mostly memoir is a series of essays detailing how she baked her way through that year, concurrent with depression and unemployment. Each essay revolves around a baked good she attempted to make, and we follow her trajectory starting with a failed almond cake to (spoiler alert) her getting a job in pastry. Each season of literary stories is followed with a handful of recipes.

One thing to make: Sour Cherry, Pistachio and Chocolate Orange Scones

In introducing the collection of poetry and recipes he has curated, Major Jackson, the director of creative writing at Vanderbilt University and an award-winning poet, makes the case that there’s an intrinsic parallel between poetry and food, specifically soup. “There is nourishing wisdom to be found there,” he says of them, collectively. The 60-some featured poets include Nobel winner Pablo Neruda and a who’s-who list of U.S. poet laureates and Pulitzer winners, such as Mary Oliver, Joy Harjo and Rita Dove. Some of the poems have abstract recipes built in. (You could probably try to cook along to Bill Holm’s poem called “Bread Soup: An Old Icelandic Recipe,” but I don’t think he intended that.) Other times, a poem mentions a soup, and Jackson follows with a traditional recipe for it.

Basing a cookbook on the specialty or personal preferences of the author is a time-tested avenue. But what if instead of seeking inspiration from the perfect fig at a market in Florence, you found it in a series of murders that started at the Fairmont Empress Hotel in Victoria, British Columbia? Amy Bruni, a paranormal investigator and TV host, follows up her 2024 book Food to Die For with this collection of recipes that are inspired by notorious places and events. It turns out, for example, the Fairmont Empress also serves an elderflower rose gin trifle … which you can now make at home! (And without any of the associated hauntings.) Some are directly related to the crimes they represent, while others evoke them. The stories are an engaging alternative to an evening of true-crime shows. The photography is dark and macabre while still having allure, and the recipes are legit, never relying on puns or euphemism in carrying their weight of the story.

Food was built into the concept of Disney parks from the beginning, and its importance to the vacation experience has only grown over the ensuing decades. But given the ever-evolving nature of the California or Florida resorts, if your memories include something you ate (mine is the Navajo lasagna from Epcot’s Land Grille Room circa 1990), chances are you can’t go back to have it again. Here, the authors have dug up recipes for more than 60 retro favorites, each with an essay telling the story of the bygone resort location where the dish was available. Alas, no Navajo lasagna, but plenty of nostalgia to nosh here.

items.title: Indigenous Hunters Drove Bison Off This Tall Cliff for 3,000 Years. It's Only the Second Buffalo Jump Ever Discovered in Texas
items.author: Smithsonian Smart News
items.summary: Two science teachers were hiking when they stumbled on hundreds of ancient buffalo bones in Caprock Canyons State Park, which is today home to the Texas State Bison Herd

images.caption: Imagen principal de Smithsonian Smart News

Imagen en alta resolución de la fuente
Imagen en alta resolución de la fuente
Sarah Kuta
Animal bones protruding from reddish-brown dirt

items.cleanReaderHtml:
For thousands of years, Indigenous communities in what is now Texas hunted bison by herding them toward the edge of a high cliff, sending the large animals plunging to their deaths below.

That’s the conclusion archaeologists have reached after discovering bison bones, chipped stone tools and arrowheads beneath a 65-foot-tall cliff. Some of the bones bear cut marks suggesting prehistoric butchery, while many others have compression fractures indicating they fell from a great height. Together, the evidence pointed to the discovery of a “bison jump,” researchers report in a paper published earlier this month in the journal American Antiquity .

Archaeologists have found numerous bison jumps across the northern Great Plains , a vast region that stretches from Nebraska to Alberta. But, until now, only one such site had been found in the southern Great Plains, which includes Texas. The newly discovered bison jump, called Nighthawk , suggests the Indigenous practice of herding bison off cliffs may have been more widespread than previously thought.

“The fact that we found this site is pretty incredible,” Tamra Walter , an archaeologist at Texas Tech University, told Texas Parks & Wildlife Magazine ’s Eva Frederick in 2023. “It’s a once-in-a-lifetime kind of site. It’s so incredibly rare.”

Nighthawk is located in Caprock Canyons State Park , a roughly 17,500-acre protected area in Briscoe County, situated between Amarillo and Lubbock in the Texas Panhandle . Today, the park is home to the Texas State Bison Herd , which officials say is made up of the descendants of the tens of millions of Southern Plains bison that used to roam the land.

In November 2021, Rick and Susan Day—science teachers at nearby Lockney Junior High School—were out hiking in the park when they spotted hundreds of bones jutting out from a cliff side, Texas Parks & Wildlife Magazine reported.

Archaeologists spent months excavating the site, ultimately determining that it was the first bison jump discovered in Texas in more than six decades. The only other known bison jump in the state is called Bonfire Shelter . It’s located in Val Verde County, close to the Mexico border, and was discovered in the 1960s.

Radiocarbon dating revealed that at least seven mass bison kills took place at Nighthawk over a roughly 3,000-year period, as far back as 3,500 years ago. The kill events took place every 500 years, on average.

“The simplest explanation for long-lived jump facilities is that these techniques were passed down over long time spans rather than revived again and again,” the researchers write in the paper.

At other bison jump sites, researchers think Indigenous hunters likely herded bison into a stampede toward a surprise fall off the edge of a cliff. Nighthawk, however, probably operated “more like ‘walking the plank,’” the researchers write in the paper, with Indigenous hunters taking advantage of the cliff’s natural spur shape to guide the massive animals to their deaths.

Scientists aren’t sure what Indigenous hunters did with all the bison meat they obtained from these mass kill events. In the northern Plains, bison jumps are thought to have been used primarily in the fall, to help Indigenous communities stock up on pemmican , a long-lasting concoction made of dried meat and rendered fat, for the impending winter. But Texas was probably too warm for pemmican, as the high temperatures would have caused the fat to melt and, eventually, go rancid.

Dense in protein and calories, pemmican was also eaten by fur traders in the North American wilderness, as well as Antarctic explorers , who combined it with sledging biscuits and water to make a concoction known as “ hoosh .”

This leads the archaeologists to posit that, in the south, bison jumps may have been less about food and more about “social or political ambitions,” as they write in the paper. The mass kill events may have brought communities together for ceremonies, trade, celebrations and other events that helped strengthen relationships.

Whatever the explanation, bison jumping was a large-scale operation that required extensive planning and cooperation among multiple groups of people. “It’s a community activity,” lead author August “Gus” Costa , an anthropologist at Rice University, says in a statement . “They require a large group of people working together to be successful.”

items.cleanReaderHtml:
AI is straining America’s open records systems

AI has intensified investors’ interest in public records. Over the last few years, venture-backed startups have raised upwards of $100 million to collect data from thousands of agencies and turn it into AI-powered “signals” that help businesses sell to governments. At the same time, chatbots are making it easier for individuals to file requests.

As agencies struggle to tell whether they’re dealing with a citizen, a chatbot, or a sales pipeline, some states are passing legislation that makes it easier to deny requests. That could potentially make public offices less transparent.

Find out how AI is testing the limits of America’s right to know.

MIT Technology Review Narrated: Inside the quest to combat Arctic fires and save the planet’s frozen carbon

In July 2021, a wildfire burned through a forest on the University of Alaska, Fairbanks campus, stripping away the moss and soil insulating the permafrost below. Five years later, we followed researchers into the forest to investigate how fighting fires could help keep that carbon locked in the ground.

Their probe revealed an escalating problem: As climate change fuels more frequent and severe fires, they’re accelerating permafrost thaw and releasing greenhouse gases. Now, researchers are trying to break that cycle. But how much should we spend, and what risks are worth taking?

This is our latest story to become an MIT Technology Review Narrated podcast, which we publish each week on Spotify and Apple Podcasts. Just navigate to MIT Technology Review Narrated on either platform, and follow us to get all our new content as it’s released.

I’ve combed the internet to find you today’s most fun/important/scary/fascinating stories about technology.

1 Hackers reportedly used an AI tool to breach US spy agencies
The tool, Artex, was originally designed for cyber defense. (NYT $)
+ Sources suggested that China may be behind the attack. (CNN)
+ Officials say it exposed non-classified data. (Gizmodo)
+ A US financial crimes bureau has also disclosed a breach. (Verge)
+ AI is making online crimes easier. (MIT Technology Review)

2 Firms tied to Alice Huang financed $270 million of AI servers in China
It’s unclear whether they contained chips restricted by the US. (Reuters $)
+ Chuck Schumer has accused Jensen Huang of export violations. (Guardian)

3 A powerful HIV vaccine may finally be within reach
“Super antibodies” blocked diverse strains in monkeys. (Nature)
+ Yet vaccine hesitancy is on the rise. (MIT Technology Review)

4 China’s Huawei has been convicted of stealing US trade secrets
It was found guilty on 10 of 12 counts, including bank fraud. (BBC)
+ The DoJ says it also helped Iran surveil protesters. (Guardian)
+ But it was cleared of the more serious racketeering charge. (CNBC)

5 Data centers have been linked to hundreds of premature deaths
The culprit is pollution from connected power plants. (Newsweek)
+ Data centers are getting their own gas plants. (MIT Technology Review)

6 Meta insiders warn its AI moderation is causing dangerous mistakes
They say the errors could have sweeping political consequences. (Guardian)

7 The ex-OpenAI engineer accused of spying has been freed
He’ll wear an ankle monitor after posting a $1 million bond. (CNBC)

8 An immune-calming pill has healed severe eczema in a clinical trial
Over a third of patients saw their symptoms improve. (Bloomberg $)

9 AI is forcing researchers to reconsider artificial minds
Some now think minds may not need bodies after all. (New Scientist $)
+ AI consciousness debates are a trap. (MIT Technology Review)

10 The US Army is about to blow up 10,000 pounds of unstable explosives
The old stockpile has become too dangerous to move or neutralize. (Verge)

“All this guy did was cheat on his wife with two employees and a Chinese spy. Who hasn’t done that?”

—Late-night host Jimmy Kimmel skewers Jensen Huang’s swift reinstatement as Nvidia’s CEO.


Kids outlearn AI—and we still don’t know why

Teaching a computer to use human language requires an inhuman amount of data. An LLM can easily churn through a hundred thousand times more words than a person will experience in the process of mastering their mother tongue.

This yawning divide between children and machines is called the data efficiency gap. It raises a tantalizing question for researchers: How can children learn so much with so little?

By reverse-engineering how they learn, scientists hope to create more efficient AI models—and perhaps settle enduring questions about language and children’s developing minds. Here’s how they’re trying to close the data gap.

We can still have nice things

items.cleanReaderHtml:
The Passing captures the veterinarian Michael Mullen as he provides pet care with deep empathy, at owners’ homes in Austin, Texas. At the film’s centre is his visit with his close friend Cindy, whose beloved dog Fiona, 17, needs end-of-life care. In their portrait, the local filmmakers Ivete Lucas and Patrick Bresnan mirror Mullen’s gentle manner, documenting this process with an unobtrusive observational approach that allows the emotions at hand to unfold with a quiet subtlety and power. It’s a sombre watch, of course, but not without a certain beauty, as Fiona is given a kind and merciful death, and Cindy offers a tearful, loving goodbye.

In Panton, Vermont, population 660, town clerk Kyle Rowe did it all. He crafted budgets, paid vendors, handled property tax disputes, and served as the town’s zoning supervisor and presiding elections officer. During morning office hours at the town hall—a wood-frame structure built as a church in 1858—he also fielded public records requests. Recently, he got rather busy.

Panton used to get a request every year or so from a company called SmartProcure for “all purchasing records,” covering everything from road salt to computers to toilet paper. Last year, those requests started coming quarterly. Then different companies began making more specific requests, like records of every purchase related to emergency road flares. These targeted inquiries started coming monthly or more. “I’m happy to answer public records requests from people,” says Rowe, who recently moved into a position at a nearby town. “But answering it for these purposes—it feels like I’m doing unpaid opposition research on the taxpayers’ time.”

Rowe’s experiences are being repeated across the US. While data brokers have mined public records for decades, AI has intensified investors’ interest. Over the last few years, venture-backed startups have raised upwards of $100 million to collect data from thousands of agencies and turn it into AI-powered “signals” that help businesses sell to governments.

At the same time, AI tools have made it easier for individuals to draft public records requests. Many places have seen double-digit annual increases in recent years. While more activity is good for democracy, AI-drafted requests tend to be longer, and broader in scope—and the offices answering them haven’t always grown in head count or budget.

As agencies struggle to tell whether they’re dealing with a citizen, a chatbot, or a sales pipeline, some states are passing legislation that makes it easier to deny requests, possibly making public offices less transparent.


Transparency, monetized

The US Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) of 1966 established citizens’ right to know what their government is doing, and by now every state has written its own version into law. Greater transparency has led to cleaner drinking water, lower taxes, and better schools. But the system is far from perfect: Many requests linger for months, the process is often frustratingly bureaucratic, and rules and guidelines vary by state, county, and even town.

This is why businesses, with the time and resources to navigate this labyrinth, have often dominated FOIA since its early days. Margaret Kwoka, a law professor at Ohio State University and a recent member of the FOIA Advisory Committee, documented the trend in her 2016 study “FOIA, Inc.”

Her analysis found that commercial requesters of all kinds—regulated companies, government contractors, information resellers—have accounted for 79% to 96% of public records requests at federal agencies like the Environmental Protection Agency and the Food and Drug Administration. What Kwoka once described as a cottage industry of small shops reselling public records has become a lucrative market for “much more sophisticated and integrated database products,” she says. 

SmartProcure (which does business as GovSpend) pioneered the model 15 years ago, with a standardized approach for collecting government purchasing data. Its requests are “handled by real people with long-standing relationships,” says Trip Colden, GovSpend’s chief operating officer, and the company has preferential pricing for agencies.

The newer AI startups promise to make selling to government faster and fairer. Starbridge has raised $52 million, including a Series A led by Craft Ventures (the firm of David Sacks, the former White House AI and crypto czar), to build the equivalent of a “Bloomberg Terminal for public sector data,” a reference to the pricey data consoles that are a fixture on Wall Street trading desks. The company describes its mission as getting “the best technology into the hands of public leaders,” with public records as one input that helps match agencies with vendors.

Pursuit, backed by investors including Bill Gurley and Jack Altman, has raised $25.5 million to help companies identify likely government buyers, drawing on board minutes, budgets, and what it calls “an industrial-scale FOIA operation.” CEO and cofounder Mike Vichich says Pursuit’s data will benefit the public, noting that many towns are seeing costs rise faster than revenues and “competition is what saves taxpayers money.”

While incumbents employ account teams to build a rapport with agencies, several clerks and county attorneys say newer startups often send many requests as they scramble to catch up on historical data. For example, PinPoint Analytics, which analyzes construction bid data, sent as many as 2,000 requests per day while building its dataset before settling closer to 500 today, says chief operating officer Mark Zurada. That mirrors the activity of SmartProcure and Pursuit, which send roughly 180,000 requests per year, according to their websites.

But the numbers can be much higher. NationGraph, which serves midsize vendors such as janitorial service providers, claims to send about 10,000 requests per day on behalf of clients; the company did not respond to requests for comment.

The requests that companies send are typically written with templates, not AI. But AI helps standardize what comes back—spreadsheets, PDFs, mailed packets—and analyze it all to create branded sales “signals,” or benchmarks to help the business clients set their prices. 

In small towns, this activity can be an annoyance; in cities and counties, which get many times the volume, handling it is becoming a full-time job. Chautauqua County, New York, hired a paralegal this summer after seeing requests double—an increase its county attorney blamed on people using ChatGPT to generate requests and on others seeking records to resell.

In Ann Arbor, Michigan, chief deputy clerk Sarah Alanis has seen the number of requests climb from 581 in 2021 to 937 last year—“our new normal is high,” she says. A growing share comes from requesters harvesting data at scale, sometimes asking for purchases from “vendors that don’t have much to do with one another,” or ones the city has never used. FOIA used to take a few hours of her week; now it’s often half her day, she told the Michigan Advance earlier this year.

The AI detection problem

It’s not just sales tech—AI tools have made it easy for anyone to fire off requests. Federal agencies received a record 1.7 million last year, which a New York Times report attributed partly to AI, as well as to mass filings by the Heritage Foundation and a rise in the number of immigrants seeking their own records for legal protection. David Cuillier, director of the Brechner Freedom of Information Project at the University of Florida, ran the US Department of Education’s July request log through an AI detector and concluded that at least 29% of requests had been written at least partly by AI, up from almost none before 2025. The AI-written requests were twice as long, and 83% asked for long lists of records.

In Pennsylvania, AI-driven activity is “breaking records every month,” says Liz Wagenseller, executive director of the Office of Open Records, which fields appeals for denied requests. Volumes had surged before—during the covid years, at the height of the 2020 election fight, or amid battles over school curricula. But Wagenseller says this wave isn’t driven by a hot-button issue, and appeals keep rising—from about 3,000 in 2021 and just under 4,000 in 2025 to a projected 6,000 this year.

While more activity signals stronger civic engagement, AI is straining an already fragile infrastructure with often poorly drafted requests. Wagenseller notes that when it comes to appealing a denial, chatbots “always give [people] encouragement to try,” even when it has no chance. Filings that used to take a paragraph now run pages. Some contain hallucinated legal citations, and one even included the user’s prompt to Claude.

On the other side of the records requests, resource-strapped offices are using tech to manage it all. One-fifth of federal agencies report using AI or machine learning to help search for records. The Washington Post reported that the Department of Homeland Security is using AI to speed redactions, which transparency advocates worry could lock in agencies’ long habit of withholding more than the law requires. Local governments are catching up, with many still migrating from email to centralized request portals. The software vendor CivicPlus says its NextRequest platform handles more than a million requests a year and uses captchas to screen out bots. That stops automated agents, says chief marketing officer Jane Snyder, but it “doesn’t determine whether a person used AI to help draft a request.”

As volumes rise, legislatures are responding. CivicPlus counts more than 20 state and federal measures in play this year, several of which give agencies new ways to say no. California’s, signed in September, declares that AI systems are not “members of the public,” though people may still use AI “at an ordinary human volume and frequency.” A stalled Pennsylvania bill would let agencies deny requests they “reasonably suspect” were generated by a script or AI. Wagenseller doesn’t think that’s the answer. The real choice, she says, is funding agencies to keep up or making the system less free, fast, and open—“and you’re giving up something for both.”

Everything’s on the table

Arguably the most aggressive action yet has been in Indiana, where Allen County officials described a growing trend in “suspiciously non-human” requests for years of purchase orders, eating up to 20 hours a week of staff time, as reported by the Journal Gazette. A state law that passed without a single dissenting vote and took effect July 1 lets agencies charge out-of-state requesters, prioritize residents, and deny requests they suspect are aimed at data scraping or phishing.

Neighboring Adams County went further. In March, it banned commercial use of its records, including resale. The county still hands over the documents, though; a notice of the ban is attached, but there are few means to enforce it. Requests had jumped from about one a week to as many as 10, often in a single burst; since the state law took effect, they’ve settled at one to five. County attorney Clayton Lengerich says the new rules don’t affect “any individual requester’s ability to keep their local municipality accountable,” only requests that “someone’s going to throw into an AI generator for some sales analysis.”

Fielding FOIA requests is expensive, and someone has to pay. Congress tried to put the responsibility on business in 1986, amending FOIA to let agencies charge commercial requesters more, but the rules were so riddled with exceptions that this rarely happens. “It costs more for the agencies to collect the fees than it’s worth in fees, and so they just don’t,” says Kwoka, the Ohio State law professor. She estimates that agencies recoup less than 5% of their costs from commercial requesters; at the FDA in one year she studied, it was $328,000 against $33.6 million spent.

Kwoka has long argued for “affirmative disclosure,” or proactively posting the information that gets asked for most. She points to the EPA, which put property contamination records online after commercial buyers had requested them one address at a time for years. A handful of states have adopted portals, such as California’s Open FI$Cal, that regularly publish high-level spending data. But this doesn’t include the full contracts that sales-tech firms often request, which reveal expiration dates, termination clauses, and service commitments.

Startups like Pursuit and Starbridge say they’d welcome this approach, and they seem confident their business model could survive if the data became freely available. “The best request is one that no one has to file because the data is already out there,” says Vichich. But publishing isn’t free, and commercial requesters also aren’t raising their hands to fund the fix.

As states negotiate reforms, the biggest risk is that rules built to limit bulk AI requests or sales-tech crawlers will land on everyone else: out-of-state reporters, academic researchers, immigration lawyers. Meanwhile, the requests keep increasing. “It’s something we’re going to have to hold our nose and continue doing,” says Rowe, the small-town Vermont clerk. “The alternative sets a dangerous precedent for a person being able to hold government accountable.”

items.cleanReaderHtml:
Here on Open Culture, we’ve often featured the charming and informative posters of Domain of Science. Each one maps out a different field of knowledge: there’s biology, physics, chemistry, quantum physics, quantum computing, fungi, and many others besides. But with his latest map, Domain of Science creator Dominic Walliman has turned away from the scientific realm — or rather, he’s ventured into the larger intellectual territory out of which it emerged. His new Map of Philosophy, which he explains in the video above, includes schools of thought going all the way back to 600 BC, and thinkers from antiquity like Thales, Laozi, Confucius, and the Buddha, who lived and died before science as we know it.

That hardly means that they’ve become irrelevant today. There still exist societies described as Confucian or Buddhist, of course, but in the Western world, we’re more likely to refer back to — and, in many cases, have read a bit of — the work of Socrates, Plato, and Aristotle. “They basically laid the intellectual foundation of Western philosophy, science, and political thought,” says Walliman. (He also reminds us that it was Socrates who said that the unexamined life is not worth living, which “hits pretty hard in the age of the distraction economy.”)

Though often mentioned together, these three ancient Greeks occupy slightly different positions on the philosophical map, with Socrates closer to the land of ethics, Plato to metaphysics, and Aristotle to epistemology.

As Walliman explains, “epistemology studies knowledge: what it is, where it comes from, and also how it differs from faith or opinions,” while also seeking out its limits. Aristotle’s rigor in testing and organizing knowledge makes him, in a sense, one of the earliest scientists. Though his body of theory may no longer be our best means of understanding how the world works, his systematic pursuit of such an understanding set him apart from much of the ancient intellectual world. The islands off the coast of the map’s mainland represent subfields still actively explored today, like the philosophies of mind, language, politics, religion, and science — which, for all its prestige, remains as subject to philosophical inquiry as any other area of human endeavor. The map of philosophy shows us not a rarefied, mostly abandoned territory, but the place where we all live our lives, examined or otherwise.

What Is Stoicism? A Short Introduction to the Ancient Philosophy That Can Help You Cope with Our Hard Modern Times

The Most Controversial Ancient Philosophy: Epicureanism

Plato, Aristotle & Other Greek Philosophers in Raphael’s Renaissance Masterpiece, The School of Athens

Watch Philosophy Lectures That Became a Hit During COVID by Professor Michael Sugrue (RIP): From Plato and Marcus Aurelius to Critical Theory

items.cleanReaderHtml:
Music is the hand of silence cupped to hold the feeling of being alive, lifted to the lips and tasted.

What differentiates music from noise is the touch of silence — the deliberate interstices between the tones, the still points in the rush of sound.

As in music, so in life: “Listen to the silence inside the illusion of the world,” Jack Kerouac wrote to his first wife turned lifelong friend in reckoning with the meaning of life, “and you will remember the lesson you forgot.”

Silence is the listening presence through which you hear the music of your own life, presence purified to become peace — a peace greater than joy and unburdened by understanding, a peace the other word for which may be love.

There is no piece of music that has scored more of my waking days and my writing hours than “Spiegel im Spiegel” by the Estonian composer Arvo Pärt, whose virtuosity with sound springs from his relationship to silence — something he articulates with poetic concision in a series of reflections recently shared by his son:

Silence is always more perfect than music. You must simply learn to hear it. Silence is utterly full.

[…]

When we speak of silence, we must keep in mind that it has two wings: Silence can be both outside of us and within us.

The silence of our soul, over which even external noise has no power, is actually more crucial. But is also much more difficult to achieve.

A generation before him, Kahlil Gibran had captured this difficulty with piercing pointedness. “You talk when you cease to be at peace with your thoughts,” he charged in his timeless meditation on silence, solitude, and the courage to know yourself. Pärt puts it more gently:

One does not have to speak.
But one must love.
One does not have to compose, one does not have to write a book.
But one must love…
If you do not speak, thinking, and even prayer, is clearer, and there is more space left over for love.

I have always felt that the quality of silence two people can share is one of the great measures of love — something the young poet Babette Deutsch captured beautifully a century ago:

SILENCE
by Babette Deutsch

Silence with you is like the faint delicious
Smile of a child asleep, in dreams unguessed:
Only the hinted wonder of its dreaming,
The soft, slow-breathing miracle of rest.
Silence with you is like a kind departure
From iron clangor and the engulfing crowd
Into a wide and greenly barren meadow,
Under the bloom of some blue-bosomed cloud;
Or like one held upon the sands at evening,
When the drawn tide rolls out, and the mixed light
Of sea and sky enshrouds the far, wind-bellowed
Sails that move darkly on the edge of night.

For seventeen years, I have been spending hundreds of hours and thousands of dollars each month composing The Marginalian (which bore the outgrown name Brain Pickings for its first fifteen years). It has remained free and ad-free and alive thanks to patronage from readers. I have no staff, no interns, no assistant — a thoroughly one-woman labor of love that is also my life and my livelihood. If this labor makes your own life more livable in any way, please consider lending a helping hand with a donation. Your support makes all the difference.

items.cleanReaderHtml:
A self is a forest. A self is a ship. A self is an illusion, and yet it is the place where we live, the costume the naked soul wears to survive in the world.

Above all, a self is a sum of selves, contextual as a chameleon, conflicted as a parliament. Which self takes the reins of our character and conduct at any given time is a function of which animating passion takes possession of us. But though we may be governed by different selves at different times, our task is to discover — and to heed — the higher, truer self that hovers above them all like the shadow of a mountain, impervious to the passing winds, holding up the sky of life.

Kahlil Gibran (January 6, 1883–April 10, 1931), who thought deeply about the art of becoming yourself over the sweep of life, takes up this question in one of his signature parable-poems found in his 1918 classic The Madman (public library | free ebook).

The poem unfolds as a taxonomy of the core animating passions we live with and suffer by — sorrow, ecstasy, infatuation, hate, longing, creative possession — each a trap, a cage, a dooming fate the sufferer yearns to rebel against. Then comes the seventh self, seemingly the most pitiable, for it is the self that appears to live in pointlessness, perpetually facing the void, but in the end the freest: Only the empty self that lusts for nothing can touch the essence of everything. (Gibran would have appreciated the Japanese concept of ma.)

THE SEVEN SELVES
by Kahlil Gibran

In the stillest hour of the night, as I lay half asleep, my seven
selves sat together and thus conversed in whisper:

First Self: Here, in this madman, I have dwelt all these years,
with naught to do but renew his pain by day and recreate his sorrow
by night. I can bear my fate no longer, and now I rebel.

Second Self: Yours is a better lot than mine, brother, for it is
given to me to be this madman’s joyous self. I laugh his laughter
and sing his happy hours, and with thrice winged feet I dance
his brighter thoughts. It is I that would rebel against my weary
existence.

Third Self: And what of me, the love-ridden self, the flaming brand
of wild passion and fantastic desires? It is I the love-sick self
who would rebel against this madman.

Fourth Self: I, amongst you all, am the most miserable, for naught
was given me but odious hatred and destructive loathing. It is
I, the tempest-like self, the one born in the black caves of Hell,
who would protest against serving this madman.

Fifth Self: Nay, it is I, the thinking self, the fanciful self,
the self of hunger and thirst, the one doomed to wander without
rest in search of unknown things and things not yet created; it is
I, not you, who would rebel.

Sixth Self: And I, the working self, the pitiful labourer, who,
with patient hands, and longing eyes, fashion the days into images
and give the formless elements new and eternal forms — it is I, the
solitary one, who would rebel against this restless madman.

Seventh Self: How strange that you all would rebel against this
man, because each and every one of you has a preordained fate to
fulfill. Ah! could I but be like one of you, a self with a determined
lot! But I have none, I am the do-nothing self, the one who sits
in the dumb, empty nowhere and nowhen, while you are busy re-creating
life. Is it you or I, neighbours, who should rebel?

When the seventh self thus spake the other six selves looked with
pity upon him but said nothing more; and as the night grew deeper
one after the other went to sleep enfolded with a new and happy
submission.

But the seventh self remained watching and gazing at nothingness,
which is behind all things.

Couple with Gibran on silence, solitude, and the courage to know yourself, then revisit Hermann Hesse on discovering the soul beneath the self.

items.cleanReaderHtml:
From plates of ravioli and spaghetti to bottles of chianti and sardines springing from their tins, Kate Jenkins‘ immersive art-meets-restaurant experience is something to really sink your teeth into. Known for her realistic knitted foodstuffs, the Brighton-based artist and knitwear designer presents Kate’s Knitalian at Air Contemporary, inviting us to consider the (rather unexpected) mouthwatering possibilities of yarn.

For the opening reception, visitors were required to reserve a spot much as one would do to book a table in a traditional restaurant, including two timed sittings. Everything from wheels of salami and tortellini to tiramisù and bottles of “Pinot Stitchio” fill the delicatessen experience in a celebration of Italian cuisine.

Kate’s Knitalian continues through December 22 in London. And if you find yourself in Brighton, you can visit the artist’s studio, which is open daily in Arundel Place. See more on Jenkins’ Instagram. You might also enjoy Lucy Sparrow’s The Beginning of Convenience, an entirely felted supermarket at The Momentary in Bentonville, Arkansas.

items.cleanReaderHtml:
There’s an unparalleled joy in watching a loved one unwrap something they both never anticipated and immediately know they’ve needed all along. These types of gifts are often the most unexpected, surprisingly personal, and typically, one of a kind.

Our partners at Joy Machine have generously curated a selection of artworks that fit this category. Priced under $1,000, the collection includes pieces by an international group of artists that longtime Colossal readers will surely recognize. From playful drawings in walnut ink to uncanny kitsch sculptures, these works are perfecting for gifting this holiday season, even (especially?) if that gift is to yourself.

Seattle-based artist Debra Broz applies her training in ceramic conservation to a practice that involves scouring flea markets and thrift shops for ceramic figurines, breaking their forms, and reassembling the figures as surreal hybrids.

Collect “Boxer Horse” ($750)

Dutch artist Collin van der Sluijs is a master of several styles, with a background in graffiti and street art and a parallel interest in the delicate, impeccably detailed features of the natural world.

Collect “White Line Sphinx Moth drawing” ($550)

With a deep love for the flora and fauna near her home in the Pacific Northwest, Stevie Shao creates folk art-inspired works through bold color palettes and arresting patterns.

Collect “Star Bull” ($400)

Japanese artist Misato Sano is best known for her cheeky wooden carvings of poodles and pugs, which she translates to two-dimensions in this playful rendition that might just make us want to get up and get moving.

Collect “Let’s work out” ($150)

Through large-scale paintings and small woodcuts, Danym Kwon meditates on the mundane activities like folding laundry or strolling around the park that allow memories to emerge and be understood anew.

Collect “A Quiet Afternoon” ($350)

Layering acrylic paint with crisp edges that evoke paper collage, Rachel Hayden blends the patterns of a summertime picnic with the eerie colors and atmosphere of fall, perfect for the perpetually witchy pal.

Collect “Halloween in May” ($900)

items.title: Bickering Buildings: A Dialogue Between the Churches of Athens in 1854
items.author: The Public Domain Review
items.summary: The churches of Athens had much to say in 1854, when an anonymous author staged a squabble between them in newsprint. Nikos Magouliotis eavesdrops on this chatter, finding personified anxieties about Greek architectural identity, foreign influence, and the newly formed nation’s relation to its past.

images.caption: Imagen extraída de la fuente original
Imagen en alta resolución de la fuente
Imagen en alta resolución de la fuente
The Public Domain Review
PDR
Eight Shadow Figures print

items.cleanReaderHtml:
The churches of Athens had much to say in 1854, when an anonymous author staged a squabble between them in newsprint. Nikos Magouliotis eavesdrops on this chatter, finding personified anxieties about Greek architectural identity, foreign influence, and the newly formed nation’s relation to its past.

Gabriel de Rumine’s 1858 photograph of Athens from the Acropolis. The Metropolitan Cathedral is under construction in the foreground — Source .

Buildings are often thought of as “silent witnesses of history”, but they have a history of talking, especially in moments of crisis. In a pamphlet published in London in 1641, at the height of the Reformation, two monuments that served as sites of Catholic devotion literally converse, trying to make sense of (and poke fun at) the Protestant vandalism against them. 1 In the eighteenth century, a whole genre of texts developed in which authors imagined what buildings might have said if they could speak to each other or passersby. 2

This was not just a matter for the popular press. The end of the eighteenth century saw the emergence of “architecture parlante” (speaking architecture), through a group of architects who argued that buildings ought to communicate their function and meaning to people, through figurative symbols, letters, or inscriptions. 3 When opinions about a certain monument or a cityscape predominate, buildings must speak for themselves to set things straight. This happened through experimental designs by Claude-Nicolas Ledoux and others, but also through pamphlets, broadsheets, cartoons, and newspaper articles that were written for a broader public and gave voice to the built environment. 4

In mid-nineteenth-century Athens, the furious construction of the new capital in the recently established Greek state produced a lot of new buildings, but little architectural theory. Academically trained architects in Athens may have been too busy designing, or too antagonistic and secretive, to share their theories in writing. But architectural criticism abounded in the popular press, often penned by anonymous authors and frequently satirical. On February 3, 1854, the Athenian newspaper Athena (Αθηνά) published an anonymous satirical text titled “A Dialogue between the Belfries of the Capital [Διάλογος των κωδωνοστασίων της Πρωτευούσης]”. 5 In it, the belfries of Athens’ churches debate current affairs and the future of the city, acutely aware of the shifting geopolitics of Europe.

Athens had become the Greek capital two decades earlier, and was the epicentre of intensive building activity. Plans were drawn up to rebuild it on a rectangular grid and expand it on monumental axes. 6 Its ancient sites were cleared of rubble and anything else that was seen as an obstruction, including Byzantine and Ottoman remains. 7 Monumental neoclassical buildings were erected to house the country’s new institutions: a university, an academy, a library, a palace . . . The small Ottoman town of Athens was trying to transform itself into a European capital.

Theophil Hansen’s 1859 watercolour plan for The Athenian Trilogy on Panepistimiou Avenue. Hansen was commissioned by King Otto to design the National Library of Greece (left), University of Athens (centre), and Academy of Athens (right). The buildings were completed, respectively, in 1903, 1864, and 1887 — Source .

Given this aspiration, it is fitting that the “Dialogue” opens with the belfry of the Byzantine church of Taxiarchs, a modest eleventh-century chapel that stood next to the Roman Agora and would in later years be demolished, 8 boasting with great confidence:

In reality, few foreign travellers (whether onlookers or looters) or local authorities were interested in Greece’s Byzantine churches at that time. 10 Systematic efforts for their protection would begin toward the end of the nineteenth century, 11 but initially, these buildings received little attention, 12 despite the ostensible existence of a law ordering the preservation of the Byzantine, Venetian, and Turkish “relics of the Middle Ages”. 13 Many of these churches were left in disrepair or demolished to make way for new streets and buildings, 14 or even reclaimed as material for the construction of new churches. 15 A survey of Athens in 1833 documented a total of 115 churches, of which only 30 were deemed in a good enough condition to merit repairs; a survey made roughly a decade later indicated that only half of those survived. 16

Pierre Peytier’s drawing of the Fethiye Mosque and the Church of the Taxiarchs in Athens, ca. 1830s — Source .

André Couchaud’s architectural drawings of the Church of the Taxiarchs, from Choix d’églises bysantines en Grèce (1842) — Source .

The Taxiarchs belfry’s braggadocio was ironic, of course, because like all the rest of post-Ottoman Athens’ churches, it was modest at best. Views of the city around 1800 — such as Edward Dodwell’s famous image of The Bazaar at Athens — show a skyline dominated by minarets, not bell towers. Christians living under Ottoman rule were only allowed to build or repair churches as long as their architecture did not compete with that of the mosques. 17 In most cases, freestanding bell towers were not allowed. The old churches of Athens only had modest belfries, usually at the extension of an existing wall, where a single bell hung under an arched opening.

Edward Dodwell, The Bazaar at Athens , ca. 1800–30 — Source .

After the withdrawal of Ottoman forces from Athens in 1833, all of the city’s minarets were gradually demolished, along with many of its mosques. In the 1840s and 50s, a number of projects for the erection of new churches or the refurbishment of existing ones began to explore new architectural possibilities, styles, and typologies, some of which involved monumental, at times freestanding bell towers. 18 It was precisely such a new construction that the belfries of the “Dialogue” were meeting to discuss.

items.title: “What Has He Done to Deserve This?”: American Anti-Metric Cartoon from 1917
items.author: The Public Domain Review
items.summary: A cartoon illustrating the supposedly devastating effects of introducing the metric system to the United States.

images.caption: Imagen extraída de la fuente original
Imagen en alta resolución de la fuente
Imagen en alta resolución de la fuente
The Public Domain Review
PDR
Eight Shadow Figures print

items.cleanReaderHtml:
H. P. Palmer’s cartoon captioned “What Has He Done to Deserve This?”, from American Machinist , vol. 47 (July–December 1917) — Source .

Wearing a factory worker’s cap, striped overalls over his star-spangled vest, Uncle Sam stares forlornly downward. He is manacled at the wrists and ankles, looming against a silhouetted background of water towers and smokestacks. “WHAT HAS HE DONE TO DESERVE THIS?” the caption asks; at the end of his chains lie two circular weights. They are labeled METRIC and SYSTEM.

A bit dramatic, perhaps, but as the accompanying article in American Machinist asked, “Did it ever occur to you that in changing to the metric system of weights and measurements you reach the very vitals of all business in this country from the smallest to the greatest?” It was 1917, and the United States was now, by any measure, a world power — would it also have to use the world’s measures?

Metrication had begun in France in the 1790s, under the revolutionary government, yet Thomas Jefferson’s attempt to import the system to the US was stymied by pirates. Jefferson had tasked the French botanist Joseph Dombey with bringing two physical standards of measurement — the meter and the grave (the kilogram’s precursor) — to America, but his ship was captured by British privateers en route. Dombey found himself imprisoned in the Caribbean; Jefferson was left without the measures he desired. Although the metric system spread across Europe over the following century, resistance by both American and British manufacturers kept customary units in force in the anglosphere. This was despite a number of laws and treaties — the Metric Act of 1866, which legally protected the metric system’s use in US commerce; the US signing of the 1875 Meter Convention , which created the International Bureau of Weights and Measures — that sought to better integrate America into the metric world. Since 1893, US customary standards for length and mass have been based upon metric standards, with the foot and pound legally defined by their relationship to the meter and kilogram. Despite the metric system undergirding these units, it continued to represent, for some, a profoundly un-English system. “Why Force Us to Speak a Foreign Language?” the 1917 American Machinist article’s title asked.

J. P. Brophy, author of the article and vice president of the Cleveland Automatic Machine Co., had perhaps been alarmed by the reports that, faced with the wartime need to read French maps and coordinate with French troops, the US Army had begun using the metric system. US soldiers now traversed kilometers, not miles, to impose American might. For Brophy, the pages of American Machinist were a space for debate. He was a passionate and frequent contributor , although his candor had gotten him into trouble in the past. (Notably, he bragged about Cleveland Automatic’s ability to produce acid-coated explosive shells — extremely lethal in trench warfare — which earned him a public dressing down by the Department of Commerce.) His anti-metric system contributions do not seem to have created as much controversy; indeed, he proved victorious, perhaps because of the efficacy of the accompanying cartoon.

Metrication proceeded piecemeal in a variety of industries, but various official efforts, like the Metric Conversion Act of 1975 and Executive Order 12770, which ordered departments of the government’s executive branch to convert to metric, would have little nationwide influence. Customary units remain a mainstay of American life, with occasionally spectacular results: in 1999, a $125 million Mars orbiter project burned to a crisp because NASA had used metric units and Lockheed Martin customary ones.

“If the metric system was forced upon us tomorrow”, Brophy had written, “it would be one of the greatest tangles the American people have ever had to contend with. It is almost ridiculous to think about, and still we have men of importance who make our laws who have failed to realize what a burden this would mean to the citizens of this country.” Nowadays, many American institutions opt for the metric system, including the National Institute of Standards and Technology. They seem to be doing just fine.

items.cleanReaderHtml:
Marquis d’Argens (Julien Offray de La Mettrie), Man a Machine (London: printed for W. Owen, 1749).

In 1637, the French philosopher René Descartes caused a stir by claiming, in his Discourse on the Method , that animals are little more than machines. When, a bit over a century later, in 1747, the French physician Julien Offray de La Mettrie (1709–51) extended the argument to humans, he was driven into exile.

Frederick the Great, whose court had for decades been the refuge of controversial Frenchmen like Voltaire, was pithy about the scandal in his 1751 funeral oration for La Mettrie, who served as Frederick’s court physician:

La Mettrie’s argument was as simple as it was radical: if, as Descartes argued, animals are a kind of machine, why wouldn’t man be? Are we not also ultimately ruled by the physiological effects of blood and humors? La Mettrie’s experience as a physician, including in the War of the Austrian Succession, had taught him that the human body, and thus man himself, had its limits. Both physical and mental balance were dependent on the health of the body, and the will or soul could only do so much. “We think not, nay, we are not honest men, but as we are cheerful, or brave; all depends on the manner of winding up our machine.”

For Descartes, the thing that distinguished man from beast was the ability to speak, which indicated the presence of a soul. Sure, La Mettrie answered — but that was maybe a mechanical issue of the simian mouth and tongue, not a question of fundamental difference. Especially with the recent development of sign language, “the similitude of the structure and operations in the monkey are such, that I scarce doubt, but that if we carefully tutored this animal, we might teach him to speak, and by consequence to understand, according to his capacity, a language. Then he would no longer be a wild or imperfect man; he would be a compleat man, a little polite fellow”.

Georg Friedrich Schmidt, Portrait of Julien Offray de La Mettrie , 1770 — Source .

To call man an animal (and therefore a machine) was bad enough, but the real problem was that La Mettrie was attempting to disprove the existence of God. In Man a Machine , reportedly written relatively quickly, he accused Descartes and other deists of being cowards and bigots, able to see for themselves the proofs given by nature but unwilling to accept them. Even in Leiden, a haven for eighteenth-century radicals, that was going a bit far. (It also didn’t help that he had a habit of picking fights in print, and indeed Man a Machine directs its ire against nearly every prominent philosopher, including Locke, Leibniz, and Malebranche. Francis Bacon, however, is “my lord”.)

The text presented here is the first edition of the English translation of the work, which appeared soon after the French. Likely on the basis of a note in the back of the anonymous French edition, the English translation attributes the text to the French nobleman Jean-Baptiste de Boyer, the Marquis d’Argens (1704–71), a fellow exile at Frederick’s court who was known all over Europe for his best-selling pornographic-cum-philosophical novel Thérèse philosophe (1748).

A breathless preface (signed only as MAN) makes clear the discursive stakes of the work, and the enemies against whom it is directed: “a particular set of men, who seem to have an interest in opposing whatever encourages us to shake off the manacles with which custom, prejudice, and education, have fettered human reason.” Perhaps unsurprisingly, then, according to Lieve Jooken and Guy Rooryck, the anonymous translator made the English edition even more polemical, perhaps because English readers flattered themselves on being infinitely more liberal and free-thinking than their French counterparts.

And La Mettrie’s text is, in many ways, shockingly modern. He was a neo-Aristotelian materialist who anticipated modern ape speech experiments; he argued that certain criminals, especially postpartum women, should be able to be found not guilty by reason of insanity. He even, like Lacan, suggested that the imaginary was primary, that all communication was symbolic. Sometimes he sounds like Bruno Latour. Yet at other moments, he is a man very much of his time: he writes of the humors and physiognomy and how, in the realm of reproduction, “the man does all, whilst the woman as it were enjoys a profound sleep, and is lost in a sort of extasy”. Well, it was still the 1740s.

Reportedly a charming, ebullient man, La Mettrie eventually lost friends in Potsdam — including Voltaire and d’Argens — through too much bon vivanterie . His publication of L’Art de jouir (1751), a defense of hedonism, was the last straw. He wanted desperately to go back to France, but died unexpectedly at a party, supposedly after eating too much truffle pâté. He was subject to a damnatio memoriae until well into the nineteenth century; today he is considered the forefather of cognitive science.

“This is my system”, he wrote at the end of Man a Machine . “Or rather, this is the truth, if I am not much mistaken. It is short and plain: Let who will dispute it.”

items.cleanReaderHtml:
From architecture to brooding skies to happenstance, the images of the finalists of the inaugural Australian Street Photography Awards highlight the humor, friction, and tenderness of everyday moments. The competition is presented by AUSSIE STREET, an organization founded by street photographers to showcase work from across the nation, which builds upon a series of festivals presented between 2018 and 2023.

Co-founder Sam Ferris says that the outfit’s mission is to not only exhibit great photos but to tap into the dispersed network of those who make them. “Street photography can be a pretty solitary obsession,” he says in a statement. “But there’s a whole community of people out there doing exactly the same thing. Getting them together, seeing the work printed, and hearing the stories behind the photographs is a reminder that we’re part of something much bigger than our individual pursuits.”

The awards opened with a show of 25 finalists at Studio 551 in Newtown, New South Wales, and AUSSIE STREET awarded the top prize to Adam Oxley. “One of the things I love about street photography is that you don’t need an enormous budget to make a remarkable image,” Ferris adds. “You need curiosity, patience, persistence and a way of seeing. Some of the most extraordinary photographs happen in completely ordinary places.”

See more on AUSSIE STREET’s Instagram, where you can keep an eye out for updates about the 2027 edition.

items.title: The Download: AI’s gas power boom and a consciousness reality check
items.author: Thomas Macaulay
items.summary: This is today’s edition of The Download, our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology. Data centers are getting their own natural gas power plants One of the biggest obstacles to building a data center is getting approval to connect to the grid, a wait that…

items.cleanReaderHtml:
Data centers are getting their own natural gas power plants

One of the biggest obstacles to building a data center is getting approval to connect to the grid, a wait that could last as long as a decade. Some developers won’t wait and are instead building their own off-grid gas power plants to fuel the AI boom.

As of October 2026, developers had announced plans for more than 100 such gas power plants at data centers in the US. But bypassing the grid brings its own problems, from worsening climate emissions to potentially higher energy bills for everyone else.

Find out how the push for gas power could shape the grid—and the climate—for decades.

A legendary philosopher isn’t buying Anthropic’s consciousness argument

Before going public last week, Anthropic named the possibility of AI consciousness as a risk factor for investors, warning that it might introduce new rules to protect its models. But that stance came under fire from an inconvenient source: one of the philosophers who helped shape our understanding of consciousness in the first place.

Thomas Nagel, best known for his essay about what it’s like to be a bat, was blunt. “Here are some of the smartest people on the planet being completely idiotic,” he said. He argued that producing language isn’t enough to establish consciousness. But other philosophers disagree.

Here’s why language has become central to the debate over conscious AI.

I’ve combed the internet to find you today’s most fun/important/scary/fascinating stories about technology.

1 Huang’s Nvidia return has lifted markets and put Trump under fire
US stock indexes had their best day since April 2025. (NBC News)
+ Trump made up to $15 million on his Nvidia holdings. (Guardian)
+ He reportedly saw Huang as vital to US open-weight AI. (Reuters $)
+ The US has also finally blacklisted Megaspeed. (BBC)
+ Open-source advocates wanted Huang back. (MIT Technology Review)

2 COP31’s collapse has revived calls to end the consensus rule
It effectively lets any single country block a deal. (Axios)
+ But changing the rule would itself require consensus. (Guardian)
+ Rare wins at the talks included a new electrification pledge. (Nature $)
+ Our climate models have a major blind spot. (MIT Technology Review)

3 Russia could launch a nuclear-armed satellite as soon as next month
The warning comes from intelligence shared among Nato allies. (BBC)
+ Such a weapon could destroy thousands of satellites at once. (FT $)
+ The Kremlin has dismissed the claims as propaganda. (Guardian)

4 Google wants to make a 24/7 AI TV channel starring you
Its new patent imagines shows and ads built around each viewer. (404 Media)
+ They would be generated from your viewing history. (Gizmodo)

5 Oregon and Virginia are suing SpaceX over Grok’s sexualized images
Grok’s “spicy mode” produced explicit images of women and children. (NYT $)
+ Deepfake porn is stealing people’s bodies. (MIT Technology Review)

6 Prosecutors say an ex-OpenAI engineer bugged company meetings
One appears to have involved a foreign government. (Bloomberg $)

7 Signal has joined banks and airlines in blocking AI agents
It’s urging Apple, Google, and Microsoft to give apps more control. (CNBC)
+ AI agents are not your “coworkers.” (MIT Technology Review)

8 An emerging technology could bypass government internet blackouts
It connects ordinary phones directly to satellites. (New Scientist $)

9 AI billionaires are fueling a new wealth tax debate
Proposals include new levies on net worth and extra income taxes. (CNN)

10 “Pervert glasses” is Australia’s word of the year
The Macquarie dictionary picked it ahead of “nudify” and “AI;DR.” (Guardian)

“The President is selling out our national security to keep the stock market high and probably for some f**king donation to his ballroom.”

—Senator Ruben Gallego (D-Ariz.) says on X that Donald Trump’s avarice is behind Jensen Huang’s return as Nvidia CEO.


How gamification took over the world

It’s a thought that occurs to every video-game player at some point: what if the weird, hyper-focused state I enter in virtual worlds could somehow be applied to the real one?

For a handful of consultants, startup gurus, and game designers in the late 2000s, this state of “blissful productivity” became the key to unlocking our true human potential. Their vision became the global phenomenon of gamification—but it didn’t live up to the hype.

Instead of liberating us, gamification became a tool for coercion, distraction, and control. Find out why we fell for it—and how we can recover.

We can still have nice things

A place for comfort, fun, and distraction to brighten up your day. (Got any ideas? Drop me a line.)

+ Rural libraries are pioneering “extended access” hours schemes to stay open longer.
+ After three years of recovery from a brain injury, a dad surprised his children by walking again.
+ Can loo roll survive a blowtorch? The Hydraulic Press Channel’s latest experiment is wonderfully silly.
+ Artist Maya Barkai’s collection of pedestrian traffic signals shows every little green walking man has its own personality.

items.title: Is mental illness universal?
items.author: Alexander Pereira
items.summary: Do all cultures experience the same mental disorders? Or are our experiences of mental distress culturally specific? - by Alexander Pereira Read on Aeon

items.cleanReaderHtml:
Subway station in People’s Square, Shanghai, China, 2011. Photo by Carlos Barria/Reuters

is a mental illness researcher. He is a PhD candidate in philosophy and psychology at Stanford University in California, US.

On a November day in 1994, a 14-year-old girl in Hong Kong named Charlene Hsu Chi-Ying collapsed on a busy sidewalk, in broad daylight, in her school uniform. She had starved herself to death. Charlene had never been diagnosed with anorexia, not because her self-starvation went unnoticed, but because the diagnosis, in its Western form, was mostly unknown in the East. Her death changed that overnight. Splashed across the front pages were stark headlines such as ‘Girl Who Died In Street Was A Walking Skeleton’.

Local journalists scrambled for an explanation of this tragedy, and quickly found a template ready-made: a Western account of what anorexia was, what it felt like, who got it, what caused it. The ideas spread rapidly – particularly that anorexia involved distorted self-perceptions about one’s body (dysmorphia) and an intense, borderline delusional, fear of gaining weight, often cued by prevailing beauty standards (notably, a cultural fixation with slender female bodies). Mass public education campaigns followed. Hotlines opened, celebrities spoke out. Anorexia became part of the zeitgeist.

Before Charlene’s death, the psychiatrist Sing Lee had been quietly studying a small number of women in Hong Kong who were starving themselves to dangerous degrees. Most of these women did not obsess over their bodies, nor fear becoming fat. They instead complained of somatic (bodily) ailments: uncomfortable bloating, a profound lack of appetite. The cognitive hallmark of Western anorexia – a distorted body image – was largely absent. Lee seemed to be documenting a distinct form of self-starvation with its own local logic. The situation has changed dramatically since then. By 2007, more than three-quarters of the anorexic patients Lee treated cited ‘fat phobia’ as a central motivation. Today, anorexia in Hong Kong is terrifyingly common, affecting roughly one in 200 schoolgirls – comparable to trends in the United States.

We do not know the form that Charlene’s illness took. What we do know is that her death became a catalyst for the rapid importation of a Western conceptual framework that reshaped how Hong Kong understood and experienced disordered eating in young women.

Anorexia is just one example from a compendium of curious cases in which culture seemingly shapes mental disorders. For example, anthropologists have documented how cultures sculpt ‘idioms of distress’ – socially learned and sanctioned ways of communicating unusual mental episodes and patterns of psychological suffering. Hallucinations and dissociative states are routinely interpreted as forms of spiritual possession across the globe, as with Zār in northeast Africa and the Middle East.

These cases are not fringe oddities. Even depression – arguably the most common psychiatric condition in the world – seems to look strikingly different depending on when and where it appears. In China, patients who meet Western criteria for depression present mainly with bodily symptoms, such as fatigue, insomnia and headaches, rather than psychological symptoms, like low self-esteem and apathy. Delusions , multiple personality and social anxiety also take different forms in different cultures.

Cultural variation in psychiatry raises fundamental and increasingly urgent questions about abnormal minds. What precisely can culture shape? We usually think of mental disorder as something going wrong inside a person, and of culture as shaping how that internal problem is expressed and socially understood. Can culture penetrate deeper, to reshape the internal problem itself? What would that even look like?

T he suggestion that cultural variables can significantly shape the internal mechanisms of mental disorders, including brute neurobiological hardware, may seem counterintuitive, even radical. But I’ll make the case that culture may possess a more substantial ability to do so – in some disorders, to some degrees – than is generally acknowledged. The basic reason is that the brain, the organ of the mind, is plastic and has functions of representing and adapting to a rich social world.

This could well allow cultural ecosystems to inculcate ‘local’ kinds of disorders – ones that may look similar to their cross-cultural counterparts, but differ in their psychological and even neurological profiles in ways consequential for scientific classification and treatment. ‘Anorexia’ or ‘depression’ in one cultural context may then be best understood as a different condition altogether in another. Mental disorders are already notoriously heterogeneous: one study of 3,703 patients diagnosed with depression found 1,030 distinct combinations of symptoms. One source of this variation may be cultural environments, including subcultures within a country’s borders. These possibilities hinge on unsettled questions about how plastic the mechanisms of mental disorders really are, and whether cultural factors have the right kind of causal access to them.

To begin, let me distinguish three widely accepted ways that culture can shape mental disorders, before investigating whether it can also shape their internal mechanisms. When I say ‘culture’, I mean a broad class of sociocultural factors, including social roles, norms, values, institutional and political structures, even particular medical beliefs and practices. By ‘shape’, I mean causally influence.

Hearing God speak seems a textbook case of psychosis. Yet many US evangelicals cultivate the experience

The first widely accepted way is by shaping our concepts of disorder. Here I am accepting a basic distinction between our various concepts of mental disorder (including lay and scientific theories of what disorders are, and what explains them), and the actual nature of those conditions. Historians have long shown that psychiatric concepts can be covertly shaped by social forces. What counts as ‘normal’ versus ‘eccentric’ versus ‘pathological’ behaviour is often prescribed by prevailing cultural norms and scientific authorities (whether legitimate or pseudo). A particularly dramatic example from 1851 is the diagnosis ‘Drapetomania’, which was given exclusively to Black slaves who fled their captors. The warped logic – which rested on the widespread and pernicious belief that God had ordained Black people to be enslaved – was that slavery was so beneficial, only a mentally ill person would cut and run. In this case, the concept was culturally shaped and pseudo, because it did not refer to a genuine condition, only mentally competent agents acting rationally.

items.cleanReaderHtml:
Rank the films inspired by Edgar Allan Poe, and several adaptations of “The Fall of the House of Usher” will almost certainly come near the top. At first glance, that story of a man paying a visit to an old friend who lives with his twin sister in their family’s grand house — each of the latter three well advanced into a different process of deterioration — might seem too short, as well as too light on conflict to translate into a conventional screenplay. Yet it’s also full of cinematically irresistible images, from the somehow ruinous yet wholly intact titular mansion to the bloodily wretched sister throwing herself upon the terrified brother who entombed her alive while their ancestral home collapses around them.

Of the twenty or thirty versions of “The Fall of the House of Usher” so far made for the screen, the most celebrated remains the one Jean Epstein directed in 1928. Officially designating it as one of the “great movies,” Roger Ebert calls that picture’s vision of the great hall “one of the most haunting spaces in the movies. Its floor is a vast marble expanse, interrupted here and there by an item of furniture that seems dwarfed by the surrounding emptiness. An odd staircase rises from one distant corner. It is not impossible that this vision, in one of the best-known French surrealist films, inspired the designers of the great hall of Xanadu in Citizen Kane.”

The avant-garde filmmaking duo James Sibley Watson Jr. and Melville Webber (in collaboration with e. e. cummings, who contributed to the script) could hardly manage the same scale of production design for their own short adaptation of Poe’s story, which happened to come out the same year.

But the resulting Expressionist take on the material has also been highly acclaimed, and through this YouTube playlist of Poe films, you can experience not just both of them, but also other adaptations of “The Fall of the House of Usher” by idiosyncratic Czech animator Jan Švankmajer and B‑movie powerhouse Roger Corman. Sensitive to Poe’s sensationalist appeal and air of transgressive decadence, Corman ended up directing an eight-film “Poe cycle,” nearly all of which star Vincent Price.

It’s fair to say that no film actor is more closely associated with Poe than Price, a link Tim Burton celebrated in animation at the beginning of his career. Price even played the writer himself in An Evening with Edgar Allan Poe, a special from 1970 in which he recites “The Sphinx,” “The Cask of Amontillado,” “The Pit and the Pendulum,” and “The Tell-Tale Heart.” That last, the most screen-adapted Poe story of them all, also appears on the playlist in various forms: an early D. W. Griffith feature, the directorial debut of Jules Dassin, an animated short narrated by James Mason, a British psychological thriller, and a transposition into modern-day New Orleans. And if you haven’t had enough Poe after watching through all 25 of these films, consider watching the recent, well-received Fall of the House of Usher miniseries on Netflix — an entertainment platform that satisfies much the same appetites Poe’s stories have been feeding for nearly two centuries.

items.title: Marie Curie Became the First Woman to Win a Nobel Prize, the First Person to Win Twice, and the Only Person in History to Win in Two Different Sciences
items.author: OC
items.summary: For most of scientific history, women who made contributions to various fields have been sidelined or ignored in favor of male colleagues, who reaped fame, professional recognition, and cash rewards that come with prestigious prizes like the Nobel. Cornell historian of science Margaret Rossiter coined the term “The Mat
